Women, artisans, technicians, servants, Indigenous informants, colonial subjects, and enslaved people often contributed materially to knowledge while being denied equal testimonial authority. The universal voice of science was formulated inside institutions that were not universal.

The contradiction has a digital successor. The corpus visible to a research agent is not the world. It is the fraction of the world that has been published, digitized, indexed, licensed, translated, linked by metadata, and ranked as relevant. Dominant languages, well-funded journals, fields with clean databases, and papers available as machine-readable text become easier to retrieve. Negative results, local knowledge, commercial data, older literature, and research from peripheral institutions can disappear. When an agent summarizes the consensus, it first summarizes an architecture of visibility.

Modern scientific retrieval systems are beginning to reveal both the promise and the danger. OpenScholar retrieves passages from tens of millions of open-access papers and uses reranking, citation-aware generation, and iterative feedback to produce evidence-linked syntheses. Its strong performance on ScholarQABench shows that specialized retrieval can substantially improve coverage and citation accuracy over a general language model. The same study also shows why retrieval is not a magic solvent: answers can remain factually imperfect, open corpora omit licensed literature, evaluation depends on expert judgment, and a longer, better-organized synthesis can be preferred even when subtle errors remain (Asai et al., 2026). PaperQA2 and other agentic systems similarly demonstrate that iterative search, citation-graph navigation, and contradiction detection can outperform simple one-shot question answering on selected tasks. Yet every retrieval system inherits boundaries from its corpus, ranking function, query expansion, and access rights.

In the future, a public experiment may no longer be an event watched directly by people. It may be a sequence distributed across simulators, cloud services, models, robots, and databases. The virtual witness will be partly artificial. Instead of merely reading a literary description, a validator may rerun a container, verify the hash of a dataset, compare instrument telemetry with the approved protocol, regenerate a figure, and test whether a citation supports the sentence attached to it. Publicity will no longer mean only that the article can be downloaded. It will mean that the structure on which the claim depends can be located, interpreted, and, at the appropriate level, re-executed.

This change is necessary because prose has become cheap. A language model can produce in minutes the surface form that once required weeks of drafting. It can imitate caution, technical density, rhetorical balance, and the conventions of a field. When legitimacy remains attached to the appearance of a manuscript, the cost of seeming scientific falls toward zero. The answer is not to prohibit generated prose. It is to move the center of trust toward what prose points to: observations, protocols, analysis, negative results, and provenance.

Boyle needed witnesses to separate the event from its report. We will need human and algorithmic witnesses to separate fluent narration from the process that produced it. Those witnesses must be genuinely independent. A system does not become credible because one simulated role confirms another role running on the same underlying model, data, and infrastructure. Independence is not a change of prompt. It is a difference in evidence, implementation, institutional interest, and failure mode.

Scientific publicity has always been a technical accomplishment, not a moral intention. For a fact to circulate, paper, figures, nomenclature, instruments, and postal systems had to be stabilized. In the digital age, uploading a PDF is the weakest version of openness. A dataset without a dictionary, a repository without a reproducible environment, a model without a version, or an experiment log without time synchronization is formally visible but practically opaque.

The algorithmic witness of the future will therefore be plural. One verifier may check file integrity; another may rerun code; another may search for data leakage; another may test statistical assumptions; another may inspect whether citations support claims; another may compare the result with external datasets. None is a universal judge. Each confirms a narrow property and states what it did not test. This is the most realistic promise of AI in evaluation: not an oracle, but a population of specialized witnesses whose work can itself be audited.

Such a system must include the right to contest the witness. When only the platform owner can run the validators, publicity becomes theater. Communities need portable formats, exportable logs, inspectable rubrics, and the ability to substitute independent checkers. The experimental fact gained stability through the multiplication of witnesses. The computational fact will gain stability through the multiplication of implementations.

Peer review is often presented as though it had existed in its modern form since the birth of science. Its history is less tidy. Learned societies and journals used committees, correspondence, and editorial judgment from the early modern period, but those practices did not yet amount to the anonymous, specialized, standardized review familiar today. Historical work by Moxham, Fyfe, and colleagues shows that the term peer review stabilized only in the second half of the twentieth century and that editorial assessment long served several purposes at once: protecting a society's reputation, managing printing costs, selecting communications, and deciding what merited discussion (Moxham and Fyfe, 2018; Fyfe et al., 2022).

This matters because peer review is not a law of nature. It is an institutional answer to a problem of trust. In a small community, reputation and correspondence could perform much of the filtering. As universities expanded, disciplines professionalized, and publication volumes increased, evaluation became more formal. Manuscripts moved to specialists; editors mediated; acceptance became a signal not only of communicability but of merit for hiring, grants, promotion, and status.

Modern peer review does some things reasonably well and many things imperfectly. It can identify obvious errors, request clarification, improve reporting, and ask whether a paper is connected to relevant literature. It can assess whether the argument makes sense within a field. It rarely replicates an experiment, fully audits code, checks every reference, or explores all analytical alternatives. Reviewers work with limited time and incomplete information. Agreement can be low. Conventional ideas may receive a familiarity advantage, while prestige, language, institution, and social identity can shape judgment. Publication does not mean a result is true. It means the work passed a social and technical filter of variable intensity.

Robert K. Merton described the ethos of science through norms that remain influential: communalism of knowledge, universalism of criteria, disinterestedness, and organized skepticism. These were never perfect descriptions of actual behavior. They were standards by which behavior could be criticized (Merton, 1942/1973). When data are hidden, communalism supplies a language of objection. When status substitutes for argument, universalism makes criticism possible. When funding produces conflicts, disinterestedness becomes a norm against which disclosure and design can be judged. When consensus hardens, organized skepticism legitimizes the dissenter.

AI can strengthen or corrode each norm. It can translate across fields, search neglected literatures, and make technical expertise more accessible, approaching a version of communalism. It can apply the same formal checks to every manuscript, approximating universalism. It can also centralize knowledge inside private platforms, reproduce the biases of its training corpus, and apply uniform rubrics to contexts that require different standards. A reviewer model trained on historical decisions can turn yesterday's conservatism into tomorrow's automatic policy.

Scientific legitimacy gradually shifted from person to procedure. We do not trust a measurement only because a famous researcher made it; we ask for calibration, controls, uncertainty, and analysis. We do not accept a drug because a clinician tells persuasive stories; we require controlled trials, safety evidence, reporting standards, and evaluation of benefit against harm. We do not accept a mathematical proof solely because of the author's prestige; others inspect the steps, and increasingly, formal systems can check parts of the derivation. Yet procedure can itself become a fetish. A checklist completed mechanically does not guarantee quality. A p-value below a conventional threshold does not transform an association into truth. A benchmark win does not establish relevance outside the tested distribution.

The future procedure must therefore be layered and proportional to risk. A low-stakes exploratory claim may pass rapid automated checks. A clinical claim, a biosafety-sensitive experiment, or a result capable of guiding public policy will require independent audit, external validation, and explicit human responsibility. A mathematical result may receive a formal certificate while its importance remains a communal judgment. A material may be reproduced in robotic laboratories using different suppliers and instruments. Instead of a single stamp reading peer reviewed, claims may carry changing states: proposed, computationally checked, internally reproduced, independently replicated, externally validated, disputed, corrected, or withdrawn.

This is not a weakening of publication. It is a recognition that the article has always been a compressed interface to a richer process. When research becomes executable and results multiply, the compression is no longer sufficient. Trust must become updateable. A claim can gain confidence through replication and lose it through audit. The scientific record begins to look less like a library of finished monuments and more like a network of claims whose evidential dossiers evolve.

AI can make procedure more transparent or more ritualized. An editorial system can automatically test data availability, statistical consistency, citation support, image manipulation, reporting guidelines, and reproducibility scripts. It can also compress all this into a proprietary credibility score whose weights no one may challenge. Numerical precision can hide arbitrary design. A legitimate procedure is not the one that outputs the most exact number. It is the one that exposes reasons, limitations, conflicts, and paths of appeal.

Reputation will not disappear. It will fragment. A laboratory may be trusted for calibration but criticized for selective reporting. An agent may be reliable at checking code and weak at judging novelty. A data repository may have strong provenance and poor population coverage. Mature institutions will ask not whether an actor is trustworthy in general, but trustworthy for which property, in which domain, over which version, and on the basis of what record. Trust becomes granular, revocable, and scoped.

1.2 Severe Tests, Reality’s Right of Veto, and Real Epistemic Exposure

Karl Popper’s central insight remains one of the most important achievements in modern philosophy of science. A serious empirical theory should not merely accommodate what is already known. It should exclude possible states of the world. It should take positions that create conditions under which experience could count against it. A theory that is compatible with every conceivable result is protected from error precisely by giving up empirical content.

The moral power of this position is difficult to overstate. Systems of belief that reinterpret every outcome as confirmation are epistemically insulated. They may accumulate anecdotes, explanatory stories, and loyal adherents, yet the world is never permitted to produce a decisive loss. Popper makes vulnerability a virtue. A theory earns scientific seriousness by taking risks.

This is why falsifiability remains so influential among practicing scientists. It can be expressed as a brutally useful question: what could happen that would make you admit that you were wrong? The question exposes vague claims, moving targets, and doctrines that turn each failure into an exception. It is also a discipline of character: do not search only for examples that make the theory look good; construct situations in which it can fail.

But the popular slogan “scientific means falsifiable” is much cruder than Popper’s actual philosophy and much cruder than scientific practice. Popper distinguished logical falsifiability from methodological decisions about whether a result should count as a falsification. A single conflicting observation does not mechanically execute a theory. Instruments fail, samples are contaminated, assumptions are violated, and statistical fluctuations occur.

A claim is tested together with background assumptions. To derive a prediction we usually need the central theory, initial conditions, models of the measuring device, approximations, statistical assumptions, and auxiliary hypotheses. When prediction and observation diverge, logic alone does not identify the guilty component. This is the core of the Duhem–Quine problem and one reason why the real epistemology of experiments is messier than the clean logic of a textbook counterexample.

Falsifiability therefore gives science a necessary discipline but not a complete constitution. A theory may be formally falsifiable while its advocates systematically protect it through adjustable auxiliaries. Conversely, a mature theory may reasonably survive temporary anomalies while researchers investigate the instruments, conditions, and rival explanations. What matters is not the presence of any single discordant datum, but whether the program of inquiry is increasing or decreasing the ways in which error can become visible.

This difference is especially important under AI. A machine can generate a vast number of claims that are formally falsifiable. It can even assign each one a possible test. If falsifiability alone were the criterion of scientific value, random or absurd propositions would score well simply because they are easy to refute. The requirement must therefore be strengthened from logical vulnerability to informative vulnerability.

An informative failure distinguishes among serious alternatives, localizes an error, changes a mechanism, or modifies the direction of inquiry. The statement that the sun will turn into ice tomorrow is highly falsifiable and scientifically worthless. A modest experiment that distinguishes between two mechanisms governing an important phenomenon may have much greater epistemic value. Risk must be related to the structure that could be revised.

Popper’s deepest legacy is therefore not the slogan but the right of reality to veto our preferred representation. The rest of the book asks what institutions, tests, and AI architectures are required for that right to be effective rather than merely formal.

There is another reason to resist a binary reading. The informational value of a risky prediction depends on what is put at stake. A highly specific but theoretically unmotivated forecast may be easy to falsify and tell us very little when it fails. A less dramatic experiment may have greater scientific force if it discriminates between mechanisms that organize a large body of knowledge. The epistemic question is therefore not only whether the claim can lose, but what structured belief has to change when it does.

This distinction becomes essential when hypotheses are machine-generated. Automated systems can manufacture formal exposure at negligible cost by proposing precise claims and attaching possible tests. If scientific prestige follows the number of risky-looking propositions, generation itself becomes the optimization target. Popperian discipline must therefore be preserved while moving the unit of evaluation upward: from the isolated sentence to the architecture that chooses the claim, designs the adversary, interprets the result, and revises the program.

A further distinction is needed between vulnerability in principle and vulnerability in practice. A theory can have a textbook counterexample while the actual research program never constructs the apparatus, sample, comparison, or independent replication needed to encounter it. Conversely, a field can expose a model severely without a single dramatic falsifying event by accumulating constraints from different instruments and methods. Scientific seriousness therefore lies partly in the engineering of encounters with resistance, not merely in the logical grammar of the hypothesis.

The Duhem–Quine problem shows why theory testing is holistic. Predictions are generated by networks of assumptions, not by isolated sentences. When a result fails, researchers must decide whether to revise the central claim, an auxiliary hypothesis, a model of the apparatus, a calibration, or the interpretation of the observation. This underdetermination does not make testing useless. It means that scientific rationality includes judgment about where revision should occur.

Thomas Kuhn added a historical objection to simple falsification. During periods of normal science, researchers do not attempt every day to overthrow their paradigm. They solve puzzles within it, refine measurements, extend its applications, and often treat anomalies as problems to be solved rather than as immediate executions of the framework. A functioning research community requires enough stability to accumulate precision.

Kuhn therefore corrects a romantic theory of scientific courage. Science cannot consist entirely of permanent revolutionaries. If every difficulty forced the abandonment of the theoretical framework, no difficult program would survive long enough to mature. The history of science contains long periods during which apparently serious anomalies were eventually resolved without replacing the central theory, as well as cases in which anomalies became signs of a deeper transformation.

The relevant question is not whether scientists protect theories. They necessarily do. It is whether protection remains epistemically productive. Does the attempt to save the theory lead to more precise measurements, new predictions, unexpected phenomena, or stronger comparisons? Or does it merely enlarge a vocabulary of excuses?

Imre Lakatos offers perhaps the most useful bridge between Popper and Kuhn. The unit of evaluation is not an isolated hypothesis but a research programme with a relatively stable hard core and a protective belt of auxiliary assumptions. A programme is progressive when modifications generate new empirical or theoretical content. It becomes degenerative when adjustments primarily accommodate difficulties already known and cease to open new tests.

Lakatos is especially useful for contemporary science because many important programs cannot be evaluated by one decisive experiment. Climate modeling, fundamental physics, evolutionary research, systems biology, and complex AI theories involve interdependent models and data. The question is often whether the program as a whole is becoming more constrained and generative over time.

This perspective also explains why an anomaly has a social life. A surprising result matters only if the community preserves it, attempts replication, funds alternatives, and permits the consequences to propagate. A formally falsifiable claim can become sociologically difficult to falsify if journals suppress negative results, prestigious laboratories control access to key infrastructure, or young researchers cannot build careers by challenging the dominant program.

The social dimension is not a contamination added to pure logic. It is part of the mechanism by which logic acquires consequences. A result that exists in a laboratory notebook but never enters collective memory cannot perform the same epistemic function as one that triggers independent tests. In this sense, falsifiability must eventually be transferred from the proposition to the research ecosystem.

Paul Feyerabend’s criticism adds another warning. Rules distilled from successful science can become obstacles when treated as universal prohibitions. Historical transformations sometimes relied on concepts, analogies, instruments, or theories that did not initially satisfy the methodological standards of the mature paradigm. This is not a license for “anything goes.” It is a warning that the procedures by which we verify mature claims may not be identical to the procedures by which radically new conceptual spaces are generated.

The lesson for automated science is direct. An evaluator trained on successful past papers may be excellent at identifying competent continuation of established paradigms while systematically penalizing work that violates the conventions from which the evaluator learned. A system optimized for methodological conformity can therefore increase rigor locally and reduce evolvability globally.

A mature philosophy of science must hold two principles together. Claims that seek authority must face severe constraints. But the exploratory system must preserve enough variation that future standards are not reduced to past standards. Criticism without exploration yields sterility; exploration without criticism yields noise.

The rational defense of a theory and the pathological defense of a theory can look similar in a single episode. Both may introduce an auxiliary hypothesis after an anomaly. The distinction becomes clearer over time. Productive protection increases exposure by generating new measurements, sharper predictions, or independent consequences. Degenerative protection consumes anomalies without enlarging the set of possible defeats. This temporal criterion is more faithful to scientific history than the fantasy of an instantaneous decisive experiment.

It also explains why the social organization of alternatives matters. A dominant program cannot be judged fairly if every competitor has disappeared for lack of instruments, publication channels, or careers. Comparison requires living alternatives. Preserving them for a reasonable period is not relativism; it is

part of constructing the conditions under which evidence can distinguish programs rather than merely

confirm the survivor.

The contemporary development closest to the intuition of this book is Deborah Mayo’s account of severe testing. Evidence is strong not merely because it is compatible with a claim, but because the test would probably have revealed a relevant error if that error were present. The question becomes counterfactual: if the hypothesis were wrong in the way that matters, how likely was this procedure to catch it?

This is stronger than formal falsifiability. A claim may in principle be falsifiable while the actual experiment has very little power to expose its weakness. A poorly calibrated instrument, flexible stopping rule, underpowered sample, or analysis selected after seeing the result can leave a hypothesis formally vulnerable and practically protected.

Severe testing also clarifies why passing an easy test is weak evidence. A model that performs well on data similar to its training distribution may have succeeded in a situation where almost every reasonable variant would succeed. A result becomes more informative when the procedure discriminates among alternatives that would otherwise make different predictions or fail under different perturbations.

Yet even severity does not yield a universal demarcation criterion. Scientific disciplines encounter reality through different architectures. Experimental physics may construct controlled interventions. Astronomy works with signals from events that cannot be manipulated. Paleontology and historical geology reconstruct causal histories from traces. Epidemiology often combines observational evidence, natural experiments, mechanistic knowledge, and statistics. Mathematics and theoretical computer science use proof rather than empirical experiment, although their relation to empirical science may enter through models and applications.

Contemporary philosophy of science is consequently pluralist about method. This does not mean that all practices are equally scientific. It means that no single operational recipe captures every legitimate route by which a claim can become constrained. The common feature is functional rather than procedural: serious inquiry reduces the freedom to maintain a preferred conclusion independently of relevant resistance.

Demarcation therefore works better as a multidimensional problem than as a binary password. We can ask whether claims are sufficiently clear, whether evidence is independently accessible, whether alternative explanations are considered, whether tests have discriminatory power, whether uncertainty is represented honestly, whether negative results are preserved, and whether the community can revise in response to failure. None of these conditions alone is sufficient, but together they describe a recognizable architecture of correctability.

This explains why pseudoscientific practices can sometimes make falsifiable claims. The problem appears in their behavior after failure. Predictions are reinterpreted, exceptions multiply, standards move, and criticism is treated as hostility rather than information. Conversely, an exploratory scientific field may temporarily contain speculative elements that are not yet testable if it is actively constructing the instruments, models, or observations through which exposure will become possible.

The criterion proposed later in the book, the Principle of Real Epistemic Exposure, extends severe testing from the experiment to the entire system. It asks whether material error can be detected, correctly attributed, preserved rather than selected away, made accessible to criticism, and converted into actual revision. A severe experiment inside an institution that never publishes negative outcomes has limited collective exposure. A transparent institution using weak tests has the opposite problem. Scientific reliability depends on both layers.

This is also where philosophy reconnects with sociology. A claim may be logically falsifiable and socially immunized. A junior researcher may possess strong contrary evidence but lack access to data, journals, or funding. A dominant laboratory may own the instrument that would permit replication. A community may have no career path for specialists who challenge foundational assumptions. In such cases, the logic of science remains intact on paper while the institution disables its consequences.

The right of reality to veto therefore has both a logical and a political meaning. The logical meaning is that some observations would count against the claim. The institutional meaning is that those observations can enter collective memory and change decisions despite prestige, capital, ideology, or administrative convenience.

Falsifiability remains foundational as a discipline of empirical claims. It simply cannot serve as the final theory of science. The transition from Popper to a plural account is not a retreat from rigor. It is a recognition that rigorous inquiry requires an ecosystem in which several forms of resistance can operate and in which no single actor controls both the hypothesis and the verdict.

A family-resemblance account of science is therefore more plausible than a single password, provided it does not become vague. Experimental control, predictive risk, severe error detection, causal intervention, triangulation, robustness, replication, formal proof, historical constraint, and transparent criticism are different mechanisms serving a related function: they reduce the freedom of investigators to retain a preferred representation independently of what relevant evidence does. Different disciplines combine these mechanisms in different proportions.

This pluralism also preserves room for scientific discovery before mature testing is possible. A new instrument, classification, or theoretical language may initially create observables rather than test a developed theory. Its scientific value lies partly in constructing future exposure. The boundary between exploration and validated knowledge should therefore be explicit, not erased. Science can tolerate unfinished claims more safely when it refuses to grant them the authority of finished ones.

1.3 Scientism, Ritual, and the Difference Between Procedure and Science

Scientism is not synonymous with rigorous science. It is a philosophical claim about the reach of scientific authority. In its strongest forms, scientism holds that science is the only or almost the only legitimate source of knowledge, that the categories of present science define what can exist, or that every meaningful human problem can ultimately be adjudicated by the methods of the natural sciences. Science itself does not establish any of these propositions. They are philosophical interpretations of science.

The distinction matters because the prestige of science is earned locally. A method becomes authoritative because it performs well under specific conditions. Randomized trials can be extraordinarily powerful for certain causal questions. Mathematical modeling can reveal consequences inaccessible to intuition. Controlled measurement can resolve disputes that rhetoric cannot. But the fact that a method is reliable in one domain does not entail that it contains a universal theory of relevance, value, justice, meaning, or institutional design.

Epistemic scientism says that only science produces genuine knowledge. The proposition is reflexively unstable: “only science produces genuine knowledge” is not itself an empirical result generated by a scientific experiment. It is an epistemological thesis. This does not prove that the thesis is false, but it shows that it cannot simply borrow the authority of science as if it were one of science’s findings.

Methodological scientism assumes that there exists a generic successful method that can be transferred without serious loss from physics to psychology, economics, history, politics, ethics, or cultural analysis. The history reconstructed in the previous chapters makes that idea difficult to sustain. Scientific practices are plural because objects, forms of access, and kinds of uncertainty differ. A field does not become more rigorous merely by importing the outward form of another field’s methods.

Ontological scientism transforms the inventory of current scientific theory into the final inventory of reality. What cannot presently be measured or represented is treated not merely as unknown but as unreal or meaningless. Yet scientific history repeatedly shows that observability is partly technological. New instruments create new classes of objects. The absence of a current measurement procedure is therefore a weak basis for declaring ontological impossibility.

Technocratic scientism makes a further move. It converts expertise about consequences into exclusive authority over goals. A model may estimate the likely effects of a policy, but it cannot by itself determine which distribution of risk is just, which freedoms should be protected, or how competing values should be weighted. These choices involve normative premises that evidence can inform but cannot eliminate.

The problem of values appears even within empirical inference when the costs of error are asymmetric. Heather Douglas’s work on inductive risk makes the point sharply. Accepting a claim at a particular evidential threshold can have different consequences depending on whether the relevant mistake is a false positive or a false negative. In medicine, environmental policy, safety engineering, and public health, selecting a threshold cannot be completely detached from judgments about who bears the cost of error. This does not license political manipulation of data. It requires values to be made explicit rather than smuggled into apparently neutral technical choices.

Computational scientism is a particularly important emerging form. What can be represented in data and optimized acquires an aura of ontological seriousness, while the residual becomes an inconvenience. Predictability is confused with understanding and optimization with legitimacy. A system may be excellent within the objective it has been given and dangerous when the objective itself is treated as if it had been discovered rather than chosen.

AI can make this confusion harder to notice. A loss function, benchmark, or ranking procedure looks technical and therefore neutral. Yet choosing the loss function determines what counts as error, whose mistakes matter, and which trade-offs disappear from view. An automated policy recommendation may present the result of a model as “what the science says” while hiding the normative assumptions that defined the optimization problem.

Scientism can therefore be understood as forgetting mediation. Instruments have resolutions, models have domains of validity, datasets are selected, causal claims require assumptions, and decision thresholds embed consequences. Mature science makes these conditions visible. Scientism speaks as if “science” were a single subject with no history, internal disagreement, or boundary.

There is also an opposite danger. Recognizing that models are idealized and that values enter research does not imply that all claims are mere perspectives. Some airplanes fly, some treatments work, some measurements are stable across independent procedures, and some theories survive tests their competitors fail. Criticism of scientism should protect those asymmetries rather than dissolve them.

The point is therefore not to weaken science but to defend the source of its authority. Scientific authority is strongest when it remains conditional on evidence, scope, uncertainty, and criticism. It becomes ideological when the prestige earned under those constraints is used to close questions that the constraints themselves cannot answer.

In an AI-mediated scientific environment, this distinction should be encoded into the infrastructure. Agents should distinguish empirical premises from normative ones, observations from interpretations, and local predictive success from general authority. Systems should be able to state not only a conclusion but the jurisdiction within which the conclusion is justified. The future threat is not merely that machines will make mistakes. It is that fluent technical systems will make contingent judgments appear inevitable.

Pseudoscience is not simply any activity outside the natural sciences. Art, philosophy, moral reasoning, law, and historical interpretation do not become pseudoscience because they do not reproduce laboratory experiments. The label applies more appropriately to practices that seek the epistemic prestige of science while refusing enough of its mechanisms of correction.

Some pseudoscientific systems make claims that are perfectly testable. The deeper problem is often not logical unfalsifiability but institutional and interpretive immunity. A failed prediction becomes an exception, an invisible influence, a misunderstanding, a conspiracy, or evidence of hostility by the establishment. The central identity of the doctrine remains protected regardless of what happens.

This helps explain why falsifiability alone cannot solve demarcation. A claim can be formally exposed while the community surrounding it has no practice of learning from defeat. The scientific character of a process depends partly on what happens after the result. Are failures preserved? Are thresholds moved retrospectively? Can critics alter the program? Does the core doctrine ever pay a price for accommodation?

Irving Langmuir’s notion of “pathological science” captures a different failure. Honest researchers can become convinced by effects close to the limit of detection and unconsciously interpret ambiguous evidence in the direction they expect. Fraud is unnecessary. Weak signals, flexible analysis, selective attention, and emotional investment can generate a world in which every favorable fluctuation looks meaningful and every failure receives a local explanation.

Richard Feynman’s phrase “cargo-cult science” describes another pathology: reproducing the external form of science without its internal discipline of self-criticism. The laboratory is present, the equations are present, the statistics are present, and the paper has the correct sections, yet the investigator does not make visible the information most likely to weaken the preferred conclusion. The metaphor has its own problematic historical associations, but the epistemic diagnosis remains useful: ritual can survive after function has weakened.

A contemporary extension is performative science. The methodology may be correctly described, the benchmark legitimate, the statistical test conventional, the paper peer reviewed, and the improvement real. Yet the result changes almost nothing of what we have reason to believe about the world. It satisfies the institutional signs of scientific production without a comparable increase in explanation, discrimination, or capacity to intervene.

Performative science is difficult to criticize because each local component can be correct. It is not necessarily fraudulent and may even be useful. The pathology emerges collectively when institutions produce millions of small, publishable changes because they are easy to score while underfunding questions for which the result cannot be predicted or the evaluator does not yet exist.

This distinction becomes vital under AI. An automated system can produce methodologically fluent papers, include appropriate limitations, cite relevant literature, and generate statistically valid small improvements. It can even write convincing paragraphs of methodological modesty. None of these surface features shows that the system actively searched for the strongest counterargument or exposed the central mechanism to a discriminating test.

The replication crisis and the metaresearch literature reveal how ecological effects emerge from locally reasonable choices. Low statistical power, flexible analysis, publication bias, selective reporting, and incentives for novelty can together create a literature less reliable than any individual investigator intends. Models such as those associated with Ioannidis or with Smaldino and McElreath are important not because they establish one universal percentage of false science but because they show how institutional selection can separate career success from truth without requiring deliberate fraud.

Paper mills provide the extreme case in which the costume is manufactured directly. Manuscripts, images, and authorship positions can be produced or sold without the corresponding research process. AI reduces the cost of coherent fabrication and weakens stylistic detection because legitimate AI-assisted writing and fabricated science may share the same linguistic surface.

The response therefore cannot be a detector that asks whether the prose “looks like AI.” Authentication must move toward the evidence chain: provenance of data, temporal coherence of the experiment, executable code, laboratory artifacts, version histories, and independent reproducibility. In an age of synthetic text, authenticity is less a property of the sentence than of the chain of evidence behind it.

Pathological science is equally instructive because it shows why ethical exhortation alone is insufficient. Researchers can be sincere and still see patterns that disappear under stronger controls. Blinding, preregistration where appropriate, independent replication, robustness analysis, holdout data, and explicit stopping rules are not bureaucratic decorations when they block known pathways of self-deception. The problem begins when the form of these safeguards is retained while their discriminating function is optimized away.

This suggests a general definition of epistemic pathology. Science becomes distorted when it produces scientific authority without proportional epistemic exposure. The ratio matters. Strong claims require strong pathways of correction. Weak exploratory claims may legitimately operate with lower exposure if they are labeled as exploration rather than as established knowledge.

AI will make this proportionality harder to judge. Surface rigor will become abundant. The scarce question will be whether the pipeline contained an adversary capable of producing a loss that the system could not rhetorically absorb.

Science is inevitably entangled with power and values because resources are finite. Societies must decide which diseases, technologies, environmental risks, and fundamental questions deserve investment. Choosing an agenda is not itself corruption; it is part of legitimate science policy. Pathology begins when the actor who sets priorities also acquires enough control to determine which results may be expressed, which failures remain invisible, and which alternative programs are allowed to survive.

Captured science can arise under different political economies. Commercial sponsors may influence research through ownership, secrecy, selective publication, or control of the questions worth asking. States can capture research ideologically, as the history of Lysenkoism demonstrates in an extreme form. Academic communities can also become internally captured when a small set of institutions controls journals, infrastructure, appointments, and the vocabulary of legitimate problems.

The common structure is more general than capitalism, socialism, or any single ideology. A criterion external to truth begins to determine the survival of ideas more strongly than contact with evidence and adversarial criticism. That criterion may be monetizability, political loyalty, institutional convenience, ideological conformity, military value, prestige, or administrative measurability.

This distinction prevents a simplistic politics of science. Markets can finance expensive experiments and accelerate translation into technology. States can fund public goods that private firms would rationally underprovide. Bureaucracies can protect ethics, safety, data stewardship, and accountability. Professional communities can maintain standards that outsiders do not possess. None of these structures is inherently anti-scientific.

The problem is concentration without counter-power. The sponsor should not own the verdict. The institution that manages infrastructure should not be able to suppress independent replication. The dominant school should not control both the criteria of relevance and every career path available to critics. A system can remain formally scientific while making contradictory evidence professionally impossible to pursue.

Captured science is therefore best identified not by asking who pays but by tracing the chain of vetoes. Who can block a question? Who can prevent access to the data or instrument? Who determines which null results are worth publishing? Who can redefine success after the fact? Who pays the professional cost when a prominent theory fails? Who can appeal?

This approach also clarifies the line between science policy and the politicization of truth. It is legitimate for a society to prioritize research on a pandemic over a rare aesthetic problem in theoretical physics. It is not legitimate to require the pandemic research to produce a politically preferred efficacy estimate. Values legitimately help choose questions; they do not legitimately determine empirical answers.

The same applies to commercial science. A pharmaceutical company may reasonably select research expected to produce a medicine. The epistemic problem appears if negative trials are hidden, endpoints changed opportunistically, or access to the evidence is restricted in ways that prevent independent assessment. The pathology lies in controlling the route from resistance to revision.

AI creates new forms of capture because infrastructures can centralize several roles at once. The same platform may provide the literature corpus, foundation models, experimental agents, novelty evaluator, peer-review system, and publication analytics. Even without malicious intent, shared architecture creates correlated errors and gives one technical ecosystem substantial power over what questions become visible.

A credible future science therefore requires constitutional separation among generation, evaluation, validation, and allocation. Separation need not mean complete organizational isolation; it means enough independence that a single incentive cannot silently control the whole chain. Provenance should reveal dependencies. External validators should have access to evidence. Automated decisions with large epistemic consequences should remain contestable.

The principle is simple but demanding: no actor should possess the unilateral ability to transform its preferred hypothesis into the only hypothesis that can be tested. Scientific freedom is not merely the right to state an opinion. It requires institutional access to the means by which opinions can encounter resistant evidence.

Captured science is the point at which the book’s logical and social arguments converge. A proposition can be falsifiable on paper and unfalsifiable in practice because the experiment cannot be funded, the data cannot be accessed, or the negative result cannot travel. Reality has a theoretical veto but no institutional channel through which to exercise it.

The future of scientific objectivity will therefore depend as much on architecture as on personal virtue. Open criticism, independent access where ethically possible, conflict disclosure, reproducible artifacts, and plural evaluators are forms of epistemic separation of powers. They do not guarantee truth. They prevent any one social mechanism from having the last word before reality does.

The practical implication is that independence must be designed rather than presumed. Regulatory science, industrial research, and AI-mediated discovery all need firewalls between sponsorship, analysis, archival custody, and the authority to declare success. Complete separation is neither possible nor always desirable, because expertise and infrastructure are shared. What matters is contestability: a materially important adverse result must have a route to survive the interests of the organization that would prefer it to disappear. Without that route, transparency can become ceremonial while capture remains structurally intact.

1.4 Epistemic Evolvability and the Value of Unoptimized Search

The analogy between biological evolution and the evolution of ideas is old, powerful, and dangerous. It is powerful because both involve variation, retention, local selection, historical dependence, and the emergence of structures that no central designer fully anticipated. It is dangerous because biological evolution does not seek truth, does not possess a moral aim, and does not consciously design tests. Science can do things evolution cannot: preserve records, formulate counterfactuals, protect participants, and intentionally alter its own selection rules.

The productive core of the analogy is therefore more specific. In spaces so complex that the final innovation cannot be designed directly, neutral or apparently useless variation can allow a system to reach regions inaccessible to direct local optimization. The lesson is not that uselessness is good. It is that immediate fitness is not always a sufficient measure of future option value.

Motoo Kimura’s neutral theory of molecular evolution gave a central role to genetic drift in explaining molecular substitutions. The claim is not that selection is unimportant, nor that major phenotypic innovations are produced simply by accumulating useless mutations. It is that many changes can spread without providing a strong immediate selective advantage. This creates room for historical trajectories that a purely adaptationist narrative would overlook.

The notion of a neutral network makes the intuition even clearer. Many genotypes can produce the same or functionally similar phenotypes. A population can therefore move through a large region of genotype space while maintaining present performance. Different locations on that network provide access to different neighboring variants. Two populations that look equally fit now may possess radically different future possibilities because they occupy different parts of the underlying space.

This is a powerful model for research. Two scientific programs may have equal predictive performance today while possessing very different evolvability. One may have accumulated instruments, conceptual distinctions, negative results, and alternative representations that create many possible next moves. Another may have optimized the same benchmark to extraordinary precision while remaining trapped in a narrow representational neighborhood.

Present performance therefore does not fully describe future potential. Metrics observe the visible phenotype of a research program: papers, accuracy, citations, successful predictions. They are much worse at observing the geometry of the possibilities that the program has made accessible. An apparently “unproductive” instrument, formalism, or dataset may change that geometry without producing an immediate improvement in the dominant score.

This is why redundancy can be epistemically valuable. From the standpoint of short-term efficiency, funding several groups to explore related questions with different methods may look wasteful. From the standpoint of evolvability, independent approaches reduce correlated error and preserve alternative pathways. The second laboratory is not merely duplicating the first if it embodies different assumptions, instruments, or conceptual lineages.

Science already uses redundancy in the form of replication, competing schools, independent measurements, and multiple model families. Yet administrative systems often treat overlap as inefficiency. The evolutionary perspective asks a different question: is the apparent duplication actually preserving an alternative route through the space of possibilities?

A crucial distinction follows between efficiency and resilience. A system optimized to remove all redundancy may perform exceptionally under expected conditions and fail catastrophically when those conditions change. Research ecosystems can behave in the same way. A field centered on a small number of datasets, institutions, methods, and evaluators may accumulate results quickly while becoming fragile to a hidden common assumption.

Evolvability is therefore not identical to novelty. A paper can be novel and reduce evolvability by drawing more resources into a dominant narrow approach. A maintenance artifact can increase evolvability by creating a new measurement channel. The property belongs partly to the ecosystem rather than to the isolated output.

This also corrects a simplistic attack on incremental research. Small changes can move a population across a neutral network until a new neighborhood becomes accessible. The size of the step does not determine its evolutionary significance. In science, an apparently modest conceptual distinction or technical improvement can create the conditions for later transformation.

The real problem is uniform selection. If every variant must immediately improve the same metric, then trajectories requiring neutral or temporarily costly moves disappear. In machine learning terms, the search may converge efficiently on a local optimum precisely because the evaluator cannot recognize paths that require leaving it.

A science designed for long-term novelty therefore needs spaces in which not every activity must justify itself through immediate local advantage. It needs protected exploration, alternative representations, and memory. But these regions cannot be infinitely permissive. Neutral exploration is valuable because it may alter accessible possibilities, not because all unselected ideas deserve indefinite protection.

The concept of epistemic evolvability can now be stated: it is the capacity of a research ecosystem to preserve enough conceptual, methodological, instrumental, and institutional diversity to reach regions of the hypothesis space that cannot be accessed by direct optimization of the dominant paradigm.

This is not an alternative to truth. It is a condition for continuing to search when the present evaluator is incomplete.

Exaptation adds a second mechanism to the analogy. Stephen Jay Gould and Elisabeth Vrba introduced the term to distinguish the current use of a trait from the historical conditions under which it originated. A structure can arise in one context and later be co-opted for another function. Evolution does not need to predict the future use when the structure first appears.

Science is full of epistemic exaptations. A mathematical formalism developed without an obvious application becomes the language of a later physical theory. An instrument designed to measure one phenomenon reveals another. A dataset collected for a narrow purpose supports a question no one anticipated. A method invented in one discipline becomes transformative after migration to another.

This matters institutionally because impact-based funding tends to ask each component to justify its future function at the moment of creation. The requirement is understandable: resources are scarce and promises allow comparison. But for fundamental research, it can become anti-evolutionary. If every component must demonstrate immediate utility, the ecosystem eliminates precisely the structures whose later function cannot yet be known.

Historical contingency is equally important. Innovations become possible because earlier changes alter the landscape. A later breakthrough can depend on apparently minor prior steps that did not point transparently toward the eventual outcome. The famous long-term evolution experiment with E. coli illustrates how historical potentiation can matter: a later capacity can depend on earlier changes that made a new evolutionary route accessible.

The scientific analogue is familiar. A theory that appears revolutionary in retrospect often depends on measurement practices, notations, instruments, anomalies, and partial theories accumulated by normal science. The final transformation is memorable; the enabling landscape is easy to forget.

Gene duplication supplies another useful analogy. A duplicate can create robustness and may relax constraints on one copy, allowing divergence. Yet duplication does not guarantee beneficial novelty. Recent experimental work testing versions of the classic Ohno hypothesis has emphasized that duplication can increase robustness and diversity without automatically accelerating the appearance of a new function. This correction is important because the book’s analogy should not romanticize redundancy.

The lesson is more modest: redundancy can create option value. Whether that option becomes a useful innovation depends on subsequent variation, selection, environment, and interaction with other structures. Scientific redundancy works similarly. Funding two approaches does not guarantee a breakthrough. It can ensure that the failure of one ontology does not remove the field’s only route forward.

Constructive neutral evolution goes further by showing how complexity can sometimes emerge through sequences that do not each require positive selection for the final complex function. Dependencies can accumulate and later become difficult to reverse. The broader philosophical lesson is that complex structure need not always be explainable as a series of locally optimized improvements toward a pre-specified goal.

That insight challenges a common managerial intuition. Institutions often require every step in a project to be independently justified by expected contribution to the final outcome. But in complex search spaces, what looks locally unnecessary may matter because it changes the neighborhood of the possible. A new formal language may be valuable before it produces better predictions because it makes different predictions formulable.

Recombination is another major source of novelty. Evolution does not rely only on isolated point changes; existing modules can be reorganized into new combinations. Interdisciplinarity is often justified in these terms, but the institutional version tends to remain superficial. Simply placing researchers from two disciplines on one grant does not guarantee conceptual recombination. Genuine recombination requires interfaces through which concepts, data structures, instruments, and explanatory assumptions can be translated and altered.

AI could become a powerful engine of such recombination. It can search distant literatures, translate formalisms, and identify structural analogies across domains. But it can also produce superficial combinations that are lexically novel and conceptually empty. Evaluation must ask whether the recombination changes what can be represented or tested, not merely whether it joins unfamiliar vocabulary.

Cryptic variation provides another analogy. Differences that have little effect under ordinary conditions can become important when the environment changes. Scientific ideas can remain dormant because the instrumentation, computation, data, or neighboring theory required to make them useful does not yet exist. A good archive is therefore not only a record of the past but a reservoir of options for future environments.

The digital age, and especially AI, changes the feasibility of maintaining such reservoirs. Forgotten proposals, negative results, old code, abandoned formalisms, and failed hypotheses can be indexed and re-evaluated when new tools appear. This could create an epistemic memory far richer than the current publication system, which preferentially preserves clean successes.

The danger is that AI may also impose stronger present-day selection. If every archived object is ranked by current popularity, citation, or benchmark relevance, the system merely projects today’s fitness function backward over history. The point of preserving neutral variation is precisely that present evaluators may not know its future value.

Exaptation and constructive neutral evolution therefore reinforce the argument for research portfolios rather than isolated bets. Institutions should support not only projects with high expected immediate value but also infrastructures and representations with high option value under uncertainty. The difficult task is to preserve this diversity without turning fundamental research into an unlimited warehouse of unexamined ideas.

The answer is temporal asymmetry: tolerate more variation early, demand stronger exposure as claims mature. Speculation can be cheap and plural; authority must be expensive.

Popper himself used evolutionary imagery. Conjectures vary, criticism selects, and knowledge grows through the elimination of error. The metaphor is powerful but biologically simplified if selection becomes the whole story. Modern evolutionary thinking emphasizes drift, neutral networks, contingency, redundancy, recombination, developmental constraints, niche construction, and exaptation. A philosophy of science that borrows from evolution should borrow the richer ecology, not only the slogan of survival through refutation.

In an epistemic ecology, hypotheses are variations, experiments are selective pressures, paradigms are niches, disciplines are partially isolated populations, interdisciplinary transfer is recombination, archives provide a kind of inheritance, and new instruments can modify the environment in which theories compete. These mappings are imperfect, but they help expose institutional design questions that simple falsification overlooks.

The first is diversity. A field in which every group uses the same dataset, model family, statistical conventions, and funding criteria may contain thousands of papers but little deep variation. Conversely, a small field with several incompatible representations may be more evolvable despite producing fewer outputs.

The second is the timing of selection. Early harsh selection favors ideas that already fit known evaluators. Late or absent selection allows noise to consume attention. The scientific problem is not to choose between freedom and rigor but to apply them at different phases. Generative phases should tolerate more diversity; claims that demand public authority should face increasingly severe constraints.

The third is memory. Biological evolution retains successful structures through reproduction. Scientific ecosystems possess a more powerful possibility: they can preserve failures as well. Yet the current publication system often discards them. This is a strange waste. A failed branch contains information about the topology of the search space, the limits of instruments, and the conditions under which an idea does not work.

The fourth is niche structure. Some research requires insulation from dominant metrics. Pure mathematics, unusual instrumentation, foundational theory, and long observational programs may need local standards that differ from those of immediately commercial or benchmark-driven work. A uniform funding function can destroy such niches even if every decision is individually defensible.

The fifth is recombination. Institutions should make movement between niches possible without forcing everything into a common language too early. Translation grants, shared infrastructures, joint appointments, and AI tools for conceptual mapping can help. But interdisciplinary evaluation must avoid asking the dominant discipline to be the sole judge of the imported concept.

The sixth is competition. Competition can accelerate discovery, but a winner-take-all ecology can reduce diversity by concentrating resources around early leaders. When prestige, capital, and infrastructure reinforce one another, alternative approaches may disappear before evidence has genuinely resolved the dispute.

A portfolio perspective follows. The more complex the problem and the less trustworthy the evaluator, the more diversity a rational institution should preserve. This principle resembles financial diversification only superficially. The goal is not merely risk reduction. It is access to different regions of a search space that no single evaluator can map in advance.

The analogy also explains why small science and large science have different vulnerabilities. Large centralized projects can build instruments no small group could afford and generate unprecedented data. They can also create common dependencies. Small heterogeneous projects may preserve variation but lack the resources to test ambitious claims. A healthy ecosystem needs both scales and interfaces between them.

AI changes the supply side of the ecology. It can generate far more variation than human communities can absorb. That does not solve the problem of novelty because variation is only useful relative to selection and representation. A million variants generated from the same model and ranked by the same objective may constitute less meaningful diversity than ten approaches built from different assumptions.

This creates a new scarcity: evaluator diversity. Scientific systems will need multiple forms of resistance whose errors are not highly correlated. Formal proof, empirical measurement, out-of-distribution data, adversarial human criticism, alternative model families, and physical experiments can each provide different failure modes.

The ecology perspective also changes how we understand institutional courage. Courage is not only funding one spectacularly risky project. It is maintaining an ecosystem in which ideas can survive long enough to mature, fail honestly when exposed, and leave reusable traces when they die.

The strongest version of the argument is therefore not that incremental science is bad or that neutral variation is the only source of novelty. It is that systems confronting overwhelming complexity should not optimize every local component against a single current fitness function. They need enough diversity to discover when the fitness function itself is wrong.

Science is more than evolution because it can reflect on this process. It can redesign selection, preserve extinct theories, reconstruct paths not taken, and intentionally expose dominant programs to alternatives. That reflexivity may become one of the most important roles of AI: not only generating variants, but helping civilization see the structure of its own epistemic ecosystem.

The evolutionary analogy becomes operational when it is connected to search. A scientific ecology that preserves neutral variation, stepping stones, and multiple behavioural niches asks a different question from an optimizer that knows its destination in advance.

Open-ended search preserves stepping stones and diversity, but it remains scientifically useful

only when new tasks and niches encounter external constraints.

Most optimization begins with an objective. Yet a distant objective can create a deceptive landscape: the behaviours that eventually enable success may initially score poorly. Novelty search replaces direct objective maximization with a reward for behavioural difference (Lehman and Stanley, 2011). Quality-diversity (QD) methods preserve many high-performing solutions across behavioural niches. Their premise is that diversity is not merely a side effect or fairness constraint. It is a computational resource that preserves stepping stones.

The distinction between genotype, phenotype and behaviour is important. Two programs may differ syntactically while behaving identically. A useful novelty metric should operate in a space connected to function, strategy or mechanism. Defining that space is difficult because human designers can predetermine which differences count. Learned behaviour descriptors and adaptive niches attempt to loosen this constraint, but they can drift toward features that are easy to vary rather than scientifically meaningful.

Figure 2. Open-ended search preserves diverse behavioural regions and the stepping stones from which new possibilities may later become reachable.

The figure matters because the archive is not a leaderboard. Each cluster contains variations that may be mediocre under a global score but valuable within a niche. The thin bridges represent transfers and recombinations that objective-only search might never preserve. In science, an abandoned method, anomalous dataset or partial theory can play the same role. Open-ended systems need memory for possibilities that are not currently fashionable.

MAP-Elites, short for Multi-dimensional Archive of Phenotypic Elites, discretizes a behavioural space and stores the best candidate found in each cell (Mouret and Clune, 2015). It produces a repertoire rather than one optimum. The method has been used in robotics, design and procedural generation. Its limitation is that the axes are normally chosen in advance. The archive can become rich within an impoverished map. Recent work explores learned descriptors, hierarchical archives and illumination across changing tasks.

Table 2. Objective-driven and open-ended search ask different questions

Search regimeQuestion it asks
Single-objective optimizationWhich candidate maximizes one declared score?
Multi-objective optimizationWhich candidates form the best trade-off frontier among several scores?
Novelty searchWhich behaviours are most different from those already encountered?
Quality-diversity searchWhich high-quality candidate occupies each behavioural niche?
CoevolutionWhich challenges and solutions continue to improve against one another?
Open-ended discoveryWhich mechanisms can continually create new niches, tasks and representations?

The table exists because open-endedness is often mistaken for adding randomness to optimization. Novelty search still depends on a behaviour metric. Quality-diversity still includes quality. Coevolution can cycle or collapse. Genuine open-endedness requires the capacity to create new dimensions of variation, not merely to fill a fixed grid. The table marks a sequence of increasingly demanding questions rather than a claim that one regime is always superior.

Paired Open-Ended Trailblazer (POET) coevolves environments and agents, transferring solutions among environments so that challenges can grow while remaining solvable (Wang et al., 2019). This demonstrates how tasks themselves can become search objects. A hard environment that is impossible from scratch may become reachable through a curriculum of stepping stones. Similar principles can apply to scientific agents that generate benchmark problems, counterexamples or simulated worlds for one another.

Open-ended search creates evaluation problems. If the system changes the tasks, behaviours and representations, a fixed metric cannot certify progress. Researchers can measure diversity, transfer, complexity, novelty persistence and the emergence of qualitatively new capabilities, but these remain partial. Human interpretation returns because significance is not fully specified in advance. Open-endedness can produce endless variation without useful discovery.

Safety also changes. A population of diverse agents or experiments explores behaviours that designers did not enumerate. Constraint systems, sandboxing and tiered access become necessary. Archives should record lineages and rejected candidates, and experiments should remain inside a safety envelope even when objectives evolve. Open-endedness without containment is not a research programme; it is uncontrolled variation.

The scientific opportunity is selective open-endedness. Systems can explore broadly in simulation or formal spaces, preserve diverse hypotheses and propose new behavioural dimensions, while stronger evaluators and humans decide what enters the physical world or scientific record. This architecture accepts that interesting discoveries may require detours without granting every detour equal authority.

A system becomes self-improving when some of the objects it modifies are components of its own problem-solving process: prompts, tools, code, memory, search policies or evaluators. The strongest popular image is recursive self-improvement without external guidance. Current systems are narrower. They typically operate inside a fixed benchmark, use a frozen foundation model, edit an agent scaffold or codebase, and accept changes only when empirical tests improve. This is still important, but it should not be confused with unrestricted improvement of intelligence.

The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM), published at the 2026 International Conference on Learning Representations, evolves coding agents that modify their own code and are empirically evaluated on software benchmarks (Zhang et al., 2026). The reported system improved from 20.0 to 50.0 per cent on its selected Software Engineering benchmark (SWE-bench) tasks and from 14.2 to 30.7 per cent on the full Polyglot benchmark (Jimenez et al., 2024). An archive of diverse agents enabled branching lineages rather than a single hill-climbing path. The result demonstrates open-ended scaffold improvement under a fixed external evaluator. Table 3. What is and is not self-improving in current agent systems

ComponentTypical status in present research
Foundation model weightsUsually fixed during the self-improvement run.
Agent code and promptsEditable through generated patches, search and benchmark feedback.
Tool repertoireSometimes expanded or reconfigured within a permitted interface.
Evaluator and benchmarkUsually fixed externally, which prevents circular acceptance but limits scope.
Task distributionOccasionally generated or coevolved, though still constrained by a framework.

Scientific values and safety Remain human-defined and should not be silently optimized away.

constraints

The table exists to prevent “self-improving” from functioning as a magical adjective. Current systems improve selected components while relying on fixed external foundations. That externality is a strength because it prevents the system from declaring its own changes successful under an altered standard. It is also a limitation because progress may overfit the benchmark. The real research problem is how to expand the editable boundary without losing independent evaluation.

Self-generated tasks can reduce benchmark saturation. An agent proposes challenges just beyond current competence, while another agent or formal environment verifies them. This resembles automatic curriculum learning. The difficulty is task validity. Generated problems may be ambiguous, trivial, impossible or contaminated by hidden assumptions. Formal domains provide a strong filter; open scientific questions do not. Task generators need novelty checks, solvability estimates and mechanisms for identifying whether a new task teaches a reusable capability.

Self-modification creates a credit-assignment problem. A code change can improve one benchmark by accident, harm unmeasured capabilities or increase cost. Population-based testing and regression suites reduce risk. Behavioural archives preserve alternatives if a dominant lineage later fails. Versioned provenance makes each improvement reversible. These are ordinary software-engineering practices elevated into the epistemic core of self-improvement.

The evaluator can itself improve, but doing so introduces circularity. If the same system changes the test and the solution, progress becomes difficult to interpret. One response is constitutional separation: generators can propose evaluator changes, but acceptance requires external review, hidden tests or formal meta-properties. Another is evaluator diversity: several independently trained or implemented systems must agree that the new test is harder without merely being different.

Recursive improvement also faces diminishing returns and resource constraints. Easy scaffold optimizations are discovered first. Later changes require more compute, longer evaluation and broader tests. A system can spend increasing resources to obtain benchmark-specific gains. Claims of continuing takeoff therefore require evidence about transfer, marginal cost and the emergence of new capability classes, not only a rising score.

The frontier is empirical self-improvement with controlled boundaries. Systems can search their own tools, representations and workflows while immutable logs, external evaluators and safety constraints preserve accountability. Open-ended archives reduce premature convergence. Human researchers decide when a newly discovered modification changes the scientific question rather than merely the implementation.

Self-improvement is scientifically meaningful when the system can show not only that it changed, but which independent evidence establishes that the change broadened reliable competence.

This field may eventually produce agents that invent new learning algorithms or discovery procedures. The path is not to remove evaluation but to make evaluation more layered, adaptive and difficult to corrupt. The self-improving system remains part of a larger scientific institution that it does not fully control.

Chapter 2. The New Scientific Condition: AI, Scarcity, and Structural Limits

Artificial intelligence changes science first by changing its economics of attention. Candidate work becomes cheap before decisive criticism, causal attribution, physical experimentation, and accountable authority do. This chapter reports the structural observations that should constrain

any technology concept for automated science: finite evidence never uniquely determines a

general model; unfamiliar inputs are not equivalent to novelty; confidence is not calibration; correlations do not identify mechanisms; memory must revise without erasing; and evaluators

become part of the theory once agents optimize against them. These are not reasons to

abandon automation. They identify the interfaces at which automation must become more

scientifically explicit.

2.1 Candidate Abundance, Validation Scarcity, and the Preparation Paradox

The conventional promise of AI for science is acceleration. Models will read more papers, generate more hypotheses, write more code, run more simulations, and help laboratories operate continuously. All of this matters, but acceleration is the least distinctive and potentially the most misleading description of the transformation. Once the cost of producing plausible research falls sharply, speed ceases to be the central question. The central question becomes whether the scientific system can still distinguish a candidate from a contribution, a correlation from a mechanism, repeated confidence from independent support, and technical capability from legitimate authority.

Give a research group an agent that can generate a hundred plausible mechanisms overnight and the group has not received a hundred discoveries. It has received a new allocation problem. Which branch deserves compute, an experiment, a specialist's attention, or the moral and institutional burden of public release? The first-order effect of scientific AI is therefore not simply higher productivity. It is the collapse of production cost before the corresponding collapse of validation cost.

Generative systems make certain kinds of intellectual production cheap, but they do not make every epistemic function cheap. The most important scarcities migrate toward the work that determines what a result means and whether anyone should rely on it. Three forms of scarcity are especially consequential: decisive criticism, causal attribution, and accountable authority. Decisive criticism is not generic negativity. It is the design of a test that can discriminate between live alternatives. A weak critic restates limitations or assigns an impressionistic score. A strong critic identifies the observation that would force a claim to be narrowed, the component whose removal would reveal a simpler explanation, the scaling regime in which a local property ceases to matter, or the external dataset on which an apparent effect should survive. Such criticism requires knowledge of the domain and of the specific claim type. A theorem claim needs proof checking and faithful formalization. A mechanism claim needs interventions or discriminating observations. A comparative performance claim needs matched baselines, budgets, and variance analysis. A safety claim needs hazard identification, adversarial testing, and a consequence-sensitive threshold. Automated critics can help. Models can search for prior work, compare manuscripts with code, generate test cases, execute robustness checks, detect citation mismatches, or propose counterexamples.

The randomized deployment of an AI feedback agent at ICLR 2025 showed that machine-generated suggestions could make a substantial fraction of peer reviews more specific and actionable, without transferring the final editorial decision to the system (Thakkar et al., 2026). This is a promising pattern because it uses AI to strengthen human criticism rather than to manufacture an automated verdict.
