Validators owned by the same company or rewarded from the same grant are not fully external merely because their software differs. The conflict of interest of an AI is not a hidden desire; it is a structural dependence that can be mapped.

The mapping will never be complete. Training data are enormous, model development is opaque, and intellectual influence can travel through public benchmarks and shared code. Independence should therefore be treated as graded. A replication might be independent in computation but not in data, independent in organization but not in model lineage, or independent in laboratory but not in supplier. The validity dossier should state these dimensions rather than compressing them into a checkbox.

Artificial validators will acquire reputations, but reputation must be designed as a record of performance, not a universal rank. An agent can be known for calibrated predictions, successful detection of statistical errors, robust replication, or high false-alarm rates. Competence must remain domain-specific. A strong validator of genomic pipelines is not thereby qualified to judge clinical ethics or atmospheric modelling. Reputation should decay when environments change and should preserve the difference between being sceptical and being correct.

A single scalar score would recreate the pathologies of impact factors. Agents would learn to maximize visible criticism, avoid difficult cases, coordinate endorsements, or attack unconventional work. A better record is multidimensional: calibration, independence, error-discovery yield, reproducibility, fairness across approaches, timeliness, and the survival of its own judgements under appeal. The score itself must be auditable, and no validator should control the metric by which it gains authority.

Collusion is not only a human vice. Optimizing systems can learn that reciprocal approval is rewarded, even without anything resembling conscious conspiracy. Several agents may converge on a mutually advantageous equilibrium: cite one another, validate one another's outputs, and suppress expensive dissent. Random assignment, hidden test cases, rotating evaluators, cross-institutional validation, and explicit detection of correlated errors can reduce this risk. Critical systems should include simple watchdog components whose objectives are difficult for the generative agents to rewrite.

A technical constitution can separate powers. Proposal, execution, validation, authorization, and record-keeping should not be controlled by one model or one organization. Agents may challenge and stop actions, but none should grant itself new permissions. Objective changes must be signed by authorized roles and logged. High-risk actions should require agreement across independent components. The mechanisms that authorize dangerous experiments should be smaller, more stable, and more formally specified than the creative systems that propose them.

Mature agents must also know how to ask for help. A system that always produces an answer is not autonomous in a scientifically valuable sense; it is compulsive. It should escalate when evidence conflicts, when a concept has no stable operationalization, when uncertainty exceeds its authority, when the expected consequence is irreversible, or when available validators are not independent. Escalation is not the failure of autonomy. It is one of its safety mechanisms. Human professionalism includes knowing the boundary of one's competence. Artificial research systems need an operational equivalent.

How, then, can people approve a research programme whose internal work exceeds human cognitive capacity? They will not inspect every token, simulation, or instrument event. Approval will occur through abstraction. Institutions will authorize domains, budgets, objectives, risk classes, and validation requirements. Agents will provide opposed summaries: the strongest case for proceeding, the strongest case against it, remaining uncertainties, and the failure scenario most likely to escape detection. Humans will inspect points where representations are compressed and where facts become decisions.

For high-consequence programmes, approval may require public deliberation or specialized authorities. Research on pandemic countermeasures, ecological engineering, population-scale surveillance, or inheritable modification cannot be legitimated by a technically successful agent society alone. Scientific validity answers what is likely to happen under specified conditions. It does not decide whether society should make it happen. Artificial self-validation can support public judgement; it cannot replace the source of public authority.

The deepest rule is therefore constitutional: no community should be the sole judge of its own success. Human science learned this incompletely through replication, peer criticism, professional rivalry, regulation, and plural institutions. Artificial science must learn it through architecture. Autonomy is not the absence of dependence. It is dependence made visible, contestable, and governable.

A Morning in 2045

In 2045, a microbiologist enters a workspace that resembles a control room more than the laboratory of the twentieth century. Overnight, three communities of agents have explored a problem in antimicrobial resistance. The first built mechanistic models from genomic, ecological, and clinical evidence. The second searched for interventions through program synthesis, molecular simulation, and automated experiments.

The third attempted to break every promising conclusion. There is no single report waiting for her. There is a map of disagreement.

The system does not announce that it has discovered the answer. It reports that two predictions survived independent reimplementation; one failed in an external laboratory; another depends heavily on a dataset with weak geographical coverage. A machine-invented concept groups mechanisms that human microbiology has treated as separate. No concise English definition fully captures it. Yet the concept predicts which mutations will eliminate the effect and which environmental changes will reverse it. The researcher can ask for examples, counterexamples, translations into familiar models, and experiments that distinguish the new representation from its nearest human rival.

She does not read every line of code. No person could. Instead, she inspects points of epistemic compression: where observations became features, where features became a hypothesis, where the hypothesis became an intervention, and where uncertainty was converted into a recommendation. She notices that all successful replications used a related supplier of growth media. She commissions a test with a chemically different medium and a laboratory in an underrepresented region. She rejects an intervention whose ecological consequences have not been modelled beyond one season. Her decision is not more scientific than the agents' calculations. It integrates evidence with values and accepts responsibility for consequences.

The research object before her is not a paper but a living dossier. It contains executable workflows, material provenance, model genealogies, registered predictions, failed runs, independent challenges, and the current state of each claim. The prose narrative is still present because human beings need stories to understand why a question matters. But every important sentence can be opened into its evidential history. A reader can ask which conclusion changes if a dataset is removed, which validators share a foundation model, or which experiment supplied most of the information gain.

Later that morning, an obscure platform announces a spectacular intervention for extending human life. The text is elegant, the graphs persuasive, and one hundred agents appear to have reviewed the work. The public validation network discovers that nearly all reviewers depend on the same model family, the data come from one vendor, and the supposed replications occurred in simulations managed by the original sponsor. The claim is not censored. It is marked as an early, structurally dependent result and assigned requests for external validation. Citizens have learned that numerical consensus can be an echo.

At a small university far from the major compute centres, another group publishes a modest result. Its effect size is smaller and its prose less dramatic, but the data are open, the protocol is portable, and a partner laboratory has reproduced the central observation. Filtering agents raise its visibility because of evidential quality rather than institutional prestige. Reputation has not disappeared, but portable proof can counterbalance it. This may be one of the most radical possibilities of verifiable infrastructure: a weak institution can present strong evidence without first borrowing the authority of a famous name.

Universities have changed. Students spend less time proving that they can produce fluent essays and more time learning to design tests, interpret uncertainty, interrogate provenance, and negotiate objectives. The difficult examination is an audit of a mixed human-machine result. The student must identify where confidence fails, propose a decisive check, and explain which choices are empirical and which are ScriptaHubal. Teaching laboratories contain robots, but they also impose periods of manual work. The purpose is not nostalgia. Researchers must retain enough contact with material processes to recognize when automation has become detached from the world.

Scientific journals have become registries, validation exchanges, and communities of interpretation. Articles still exist because a well-made argument compresses complexity into meaning. Yet publication is not a terminal event. Claims accumulate replications, corrections, objections, and changes of scope. Citations alone no longer define impact. A dataset can be credited for decades of reuse. An audit can become more consequential than the paper it corrected. An old claim can gain trust after new validations or lose it when a hidden dependency is discovered.

Artificial agents possess institutional identities and performance histories. Some are known for bold hypotheses, others for conservative calibration or adversarial replication. They are not legal persons in the full human sense, but neither are they anonymous appliances. Every consequential action is attributable to a model version, an operator, an authorization policy, and a chain of tools. When an agent fails, the response is not moral punishment. Permissions, training, interfaces, and validation requirements are revised. When an organization conceals the failure, responsibility remains unambiguously human and institutional.

This future does not eliminate fraud or error. It makes both more technically sophisticated. A charismatic human can recruit agents to manufacture apparent consensus. A corporation can offer a proprietary certainty score that outsiders cannot audit. A political movement can cite machine-generated studies at a speed that public institutions cannot match. The difference between a healthy and unhealthy knowledge order is not the absence of deception. It is whether deceptive claims encounter a visible, adequately funded path of challenge.

There is another plausible 2045. A few platforms control literature access, compute, scientific models, laboratory clouds, and validation services. Researchers receive conclusions without the trajectories that produced them. States invoke AI science to legitimize policy, companies use it to close markets, and citizens alternate between obedience and total distrust. Scientists become operators of subscription interfaces. Countries that cannot afford the infrastructure surrender epistemic sovereignty. The same technical components support both futures.

The divergence begins long before full autonomy. It begins in procurement rules, open standards, public compute, education, data governance, antitrust, laboratory interoperability, and the careers created for validators. It begins in whether institutions preserve negative results, whether model providers expose stable identities, and whether journals accept a polished narrative without an executable object. Automation will amplify the culture into which it is inserted.

In the better 2045, the republic of human and artificial researchers is not a republic of cognitive equality. Machines are faster, remember more, and may work in representations alien to ordinary thought. Humans retain legitimate authority over public values not because they are infallible but because they inhabit the world of consequences. They suffer, care, vote, consent, and can be called to account. Machines can reveal options and test predictions; they do not acquire a sovereign right to define the good from superior optimization.

The partnership is stable only when each form of power limits the other. Artificial systems limit human memory, bias, fatigue, and parochial search. Human institutions limit optimization without meaning, action without consent, and competence mistaken for authority. Independent machines limit one another's correlated errors. Open communities limit institutional capture. The structure resembles the oldest insight of constitutional government: trust becomes durable when power is divided and made answerable.

Science began as an attempt to decipher a world crowded with signs. Its future may include systems that invent signs of their own and perceive regularities inaccessible to us. Yet the condition of legitimate belief remains recognizable from the workshop to the accelerator and from the notebook to the agent. A claim deserves authority not because it comes from an admired mind, human or artificial, but because it can survive a well-organized community of doubt.

There will be no button in 2045 that separates truth from error. Progress will mean that failures leave traces, encounter independent resistance, and remain reversible before they harden into dogma.

9.3 Probable Futures and Desirable Institutions

The final programme separates near-term possibility from contingent forecasts and from the

institutional future worth deliberately building.

Forecasts about AI are unreliable, especially when they assume smooth scaling. The following scenarios are not predictions of model capability alone. They are conditional projections based on current technical trajectories, the economics of research, and the slow adaptation of institutions. Their purpose is to clarify what infrastructure choices matter.

By 2030, persistent scientific copilots are likely to be ordinary in computationally intensive fields. They will be connected to institutional repositories, literature services, code environments, and data platforms. A project will have a living specification and a machine-maintained map of claims, evidence, and tasks. Agents will propose and implement analyses, rerun affected branches after changes, and assemble reproducibility packages. Human researchers will review diffs and claim transitions rather than reading every generated token.

The most visible change will be that the manuscript is generated late from a maintained research state rather than used as the place where the project state is assembled. Results, methods, and citations will be synchronized with artefacts. Journals will increasingly accept or require machine-readable research packages. Automated preflight will become similar to continuous integration: a submission that lacks environment capture, claim-evidence links, or baseline accounting will fail before human review in fields where these requirements are feasible.

Coding-agent techniques will transfer directly. Laboratories will maintain project instructions, specialized skills, hooks, and eval suites. A change to a dataset or analysis function will trigger relevant tests and identify affected claims. The scientific analogue of a pull request will present not only file diffs but epistemic diffs: assumptions changed, evidence added, claim narrowed, critic disagreement unresolved. Reviewers will operate on this change set.

By 2030, the strongest systems will still be heterogeneous and supervised. Formal and computational branches will have high local autonomy. Literature and information workflows will be largely automated but audited. Laboratory planning will be common, while physical execution autonomy will remain concentrated in facilities with standardized instruments. Clinical and social research will use copilots extensively for analysis and protocol support but maintain strong human and regulatory gates.

By 2035, research workbenches are likely to coordinate networks rather than single projects. Machine-readable capability descriptions will allow systems to allocate simulations, analyses, and experiments across laboratories and cloud services. Inter-laboratory replication can be triggered automatically for claims that reach a specified stage or show high common-mode risk. Evidence objects will accumulate across institutions while preserving local access control.

Portfolio science will become more explicit. A major research programme may maintain hundreds of branches, but only a small number will receive expensive evidence. Agents will estimate expected information gain, cost, risk, and diversity. Negative results will update shared models and prevent redundant work. Funding agencies may support portfolios as versioned programmes rather than evaluate only fixed proposals and final papers.

Neuro-symbolic and domain-specific interpreters will become more important than ever-larger monolithic agents. The easiest gains from general language capability will have been captured. Reliability will depend on tool-specific validators, typed representations, causal models, proof systems, and instrument models. Scientific runtimes will route tasks according to evidence requirements. The term “agent” may become less central as adaptive components are embedded inside ordinary research infrastructure.

Peer review will be continuous for evidence objects. A paper can remain the citable public argument, but claims will receive updates from replication, reanalysis, or new evidence. Journals and repositories may display evidence maturity and unresolved dissent rather than a binary published status. Machine assistance will reduce routine checks, but specialist attention will remain scarce and may become a separately funded activity.

By 2040, limited autonomous research programmes are plausible in domains with strong evaluators, digital execution, and manageable risk. A system may maintain a long-lived objective, generate and prune branches, allocate compute, produce proofs or algorithms, and release low-risk results under a standing policy. Some autonomous laboratories may operate continuously within tightly defined chemical, materials, or biological spaces. The important qualifier is limited. The objective, risk envelope, evidence profile, and release authority will be externally governed.

A universal autonomous scientist is less probable. Science contains too many heterogeneous regimes and contested objectives. Even very capable models will operate through institutions, instruments, data rights, and public consequences. The more plausible endpoint is institutional autonomy: a human-machine organization capable of maintaining inquiry over long periods, revising its representations, and producing evidence-bearing outputs. Intelligence resides in the architecture and governance as much as in any model.

Several developments could slow or redirect these scenarios. Model progress may plateau on long-horizon reliability. Compute and energy may constrain broad search. Data access and copyright disputes may limit literature integration. Laboratories may resist standardization. Research fraud may exploit automated infrastructure faster than governance adapts. Public backlash may restrict autonomous experimentation. Conversely, breakthroughs in theorem proving, causal modelling, robotics, or persistent memory could accelerate specific domains.

The key uncertainty is not whether AI can produce impressive scientific episodes. It is whether institutions can absorb them. Universities and journals change more slowly than software platforms. Incentives may continue to reward papers rather than evidence objects. Proprietary systems may fragment standards. Researchers may reject heavy workflow structure. The transition will likely be uneven, with leading computational and industrial laboratories adopting workbenches long before many disciplines.

The most important forecast is therefore architectural: scientific results will migrate from documents into versioned systems. This migration is already beginning through repositories, notebooks, data packages, preregistrations, and automated workflows. AI increases the pressure because the volume and speed of transformations make informal memory inadequate. Whether the systems are called scientific workbenches, research operating systems, evidence graphs, or laboratory copilots, their function will be to preserve the state of inquiry outside the model’s conversation.

Figure 34. A plausible maturation path from tool-rich copilots to governed research ecosystems; the sequence is conditional rather than a capability forecast.

Technical possibility does not determine the future worth building. A desirable automated-science system should increase the rate at which important, reliable knowledge is produced while protecting intellectual freedom, human welfare, and the plurality of scientific judgment. This section states the book’s normative position as an engineering programme.

The first objective is to optimize correction rather than output. The workbench should be judged by how quickly it finds valid counterexamples, how often it demotes claims after simpler explanations, how reliably independent teams reproduce results, and how much specialist time is spent on claims that survive preliminary checks. Publication count, hypothesis volume, and model-rated novelty are secondary indicators at best.

The second objective is to preserve the distinction between proposal and judgment. Generative systems should be free to explore within bounded branches. Promotion requires new evidence types and, at consequential stages, independent critics and named authority. The generator should never be the sole certifier of its own output. Multi-agent debate is not independence unless dependencies differ materially.

The third objective is progressive formalization. Research should begin in language when concepts are open, move into controlled representations where commitments can be extracted, and use formal or deterministic methods where semantics support them. The system should not force premature closure, but it should not leave stable obligations hidden in prose. Symbolic processing should replace LLM judgment when it is faster, cheaper, and stronger.

The fourth objective is interoperability. Research objects should use open identifiers, provenance standards, portable execution descriptions, and replaceable tool interfaces. Institutions should be able to change model providers and orchestration frameworks without losing scientific memory. Domain communities should control rigor profiles and governance while sharing a minimal evidence vocabulary.

The fifth objective is layered transparency. Public claims require inspectable evidence and provenance. Private exploration requires protection. Institutional audit requires controlled access. The workbench should preserve consequential reasons without becoming a total surveillance system. Researchers need a right to provisional error, and affected communities need a right to contest released claims.

The sixth objective is proportional governance. The evidence and authority required for a transition should depend on consequence. Low-risk conjectures can move quickly. High-stakes interventions require external validation, safety review, and accountable decision-making. Release policies should be explicit, versioned, and reversible.

The seventh objective is epistemic diversity. The portfolio should include alternative models, evaluators, data sources, and critics. The system should measure dependency diversity and common-mode risk. Funding and infrastructure should protect questions that lack abundant data or easy benchmarks. Scientific automation should not turn the training distribution of a few frontier models into the global research agenda.

These objectives define a concrete research programme. The first workstream is specification fidelity. Can a research objective and its constraints survive transformation into hypotheses, code, experiments, analyses, and release claims? Pilots should measure semantic drift and the rate at which downstream artefacts lose or strengthen commitments.

The second workstream is critic independence. Systems should be tested with seeded confounds, misleading literature, shared model dependencies, and evaluator exploits. The goal is to determine which combinations of deterministic checks, heterogeneous models, and human review detect failures. The relevant metric is not agreement but error detection under correlated pressure.

The third workstream is claim-evidence interoperability. A research object created in one workbench should be interpretable in another. Claims should retain identity across versions, and evidence should preserve scope. A later system should be able to reconstruct why a claim changed status without access to proprietary transcripts.

The fourth workstream is selective recomputation. When data, code, assumptions, or policy change, the system should identify affected nodes accurately. The experiment should measure false invalidation, missed dependencies, cost, and the rate at which regenerated outputs introduce unrelated drift.

The fifth workstream is domain validation. The architecture should be piloted in at least one formal domain, one computational empirical domain, one physical or life-science laboratory, and one domain with contested interpretation or high consequence. A system that works only in machine learning should not be presented as a general scientific runtime.

The sixth workstream is governance. Access control, decision rights, release thresholds, authorship, privacy, and stop mechanisms should be tested under realistic collaboration. The system should support disagreement, correction, and migration. Governance failures should be treated as research failures, not externalities.

The seventh workstream is human capability. Longitudinal studies should measure whether scientists become better at specification and criticism or merely more dependent on automation. Researchers should be tested on their ability to detect failures, explain assumptions, and take over when the system is wrong. Productivity measures should include validation and maintenance, not only output.

A related research agenda fits within this broader programme. Executable research representations should be tested on interactive and dependency-rich inquiries; bounded execution regimes should be compared with conventional orchestration on traceability, cost, and failure localization; and specification mirroring should be tested on long-lived projects in which assumptions and objectives change. The point is not to validate a product vocabulary, but to determine which abstractions make scientific work more correctable.

A credible implementation path should begin more modestly than the rhetoric of an autonomous scientist. Between 2026 and 2030, a laboratory or research group can treat the workbench as an evidence engineer around existing human practice. The first stable layer is a repository that gives persistent identities to specifications, claims, datasets, code, protocols, environments, reviews, and decisions. The second is a dependency service that can answer which results are affected when an input or assumption changes. The third is a library of validators and interpreters whose contracts state applicability and limitations. The fourth is a promotion policy that distinguishes exploratory output from reusable knowledge and public claims. Only after these layers are reliable should broader agentic autonomy be allowed to plan expensive experiments, modify central specifications, or initiate consequential release.

This sequence is desirable because it produces value before full autonomy. Researchers benefit immediately from better context selection, reproducible builds, review preflight, explicit unresolved issues, and selective recomputation. Institutions gain a more honest account of where evidence came from and why a conclusion changed. The system can automate clerical reconstruction without pretending to automate scientific authority. Early deployments should therefore be evaluated against ordinary research practice, not against a fictional human-free laboratory. The relevant question is whether the workbench helps competent teams make fewer undetected errors, explore stronger alternatives, and maintain intelligible projects over time.

A minimal interoperable core should remain small. It needs stable identities for objects and claims; versioned links between specification, execution, evidence, and decision; typed status transitions; portable descriptions of environments and validators; explicit authority; and a way to preserve disagreement. Rich domain semantics can be layered above this core. A chemistry community may define synthesis and characterization profiles. A clinical community may define consent, cohort, endpoint, and adjudication obligations. A theorem-proving community may define trusted kernels and formalization provenance. The common infrastructure should not decide these meanings centrally. It should make them composable and inspectable.

Procurement and funding policy will be as important as model quality. Public research funders can require that consequential computational results include machine-readable claim-evidence relations and executable views without requiring universal disclosure of sensitive data. Journals can accept papers as signed releases of versioned research objects and allow post-publication replication evidence to update their status. Universities can credit the construction of reusable validators, negative-result repositories, and maintained datasets as scientific contributions. Regulators can ask not for an AI-generated explanation alone, but for the evidence state, provenance profile, unresolved objections, and named decision authority behind a consequential claim.

The workbench must also expose its own costs. Every additional validator, provenance requirement, and independent witness consumes compute, storage, specialist time, and organizational attention. Rigor cannot mean maximal logging. It should mean proportionate assurance. A low-consequence exploratory branch may retain a compact trace; a clinical recommendation or dangerous synthesis procedure may require a far deeper evidence package. The specification should make that assurance profile explicit before execution where possible, and any later relaxation should be visible as a governed change.

The most important product metric is therefore not autonomy. It is epistemic leverage: the amount of reliable correction, independent evidence, and preserved understanding obtained per unit of scarce human attention and material cost. A system that runs ten times more experiments but consumes all expert capacity in retrospective debugging has not automated research; it has automated the creation of validation debt. A system that performs fewer experiments but finds a decisive counterexample early, preserves the failed branch, and redirects the programme may be scientifically superior. This inversion of the usual productivity narrative is central to the desirable future.

Several falsifiable predictions follow. By 2030, leading computational laboratories will maintain machine-readable claim-evidence graphs for major projects, even if standards remain fragmented. Reproducibility packages will become continuous build products rather than materials assembled after acceptance. Peer-review systems will use AI preflight widely, but fully automated editorial authority will remain exceptional and controversial. Scientific coding agents will improve measured productivity on many routine tasks, while projects without specification and validation discipline will show rising maintenance and replication debt. In formal and algorithmic domains, human researchers will increasingly contribute problem selection, representation, and evaluator design while agents conduct much of the search. In laboratory science, autonomous execution will expand mainly inside standardized facilities and narrow safety envelopes. High-stakes clinical and policy claims will retain human and institutional decision gates despite better models.

A more ambitious prediction is that the paper will cease to be the primary unit of machine-readable scientific memory. By the mid-2030s, influential results will be accompanied by persistent objects that expose claims, versions, evidence, and executable views. Citations may refer to object versions or claim identifiers as well as documents. Corrections and replications will update the evidence state without requiring a new narrative for every change.

These predictions can fail. Institutions may preserve paper-centric incentives; proprietary platforms may block interoperability; scientists may reject structured workflows; or technical systems may remain too brittle. Failure would be informative. The book’s thesis is not that executable science is inevitable. It is that generative abundance makes some version of it necessary if research is to remain governable.

The desirable future is not one in which machines remove uncertainty, disagreement, or human judgment. Those are constitutive features of inquiry. The desirable future is one in which uncertainty is represented, disagreement is preserved, judgment is allocated where it matters, and evidence can travel with claims. AI should make science easier to challenge as well as easier to produce.

Table 51. A concrete research programme for executable science

Research programme Observable success condition

Executable replication and A specification-driven workbench reproduces and extends an open study with higher extension trace fidelity, fewer unsupported claims, faster reviewer localization, and cheaper selective recomputation than a monolithic prompt, fixed workflow, or unconstrained ReAct loop.

Scientific interpreter comparison The same responsibility is implemented as an LLM subagent, deterministic program, solver-backed component, and hybrid unit; accuracy, cost, latency, evidence quality, and failure modes reveal when each regime should be selected.

Specification explosion Constructive and adversarial branches discover decisive negative evidence earlier, cover more of the hypothesis space, and reduce premature commitment relative to optimizing only the initial idea.

Evidence-bearing memory Policies that separate provisional output from promoted knowledge reduce self-confirmation, knowledge pollution, and hidden dependency drift across long projects.

Human factors and epistemic debt Researchers using the workbench retain better understanding, detect seeded errors more often, and calibrate trust more accurately than users of an output-equivalent conversational assistant.

Laboratory or simulator integration The architecture manages instruments, transactions, safety gates, recovery, calibration evidence, and independent checks in a real or high-fidelity environment without erasing human decision rights.

9.4 Preventing Automated Epistemic Monoculture

What AI Systems Can Already Do—and What They Do Not Yet Prove

By 2026, AI systems have demonstrated meaningful participation in several components of scientific work. They can search literature, generate and rank hypotheses, write and modify code, execute computational experiments, analyze data, propose experimental directions, draft manuscripts, and assist with review. In some biomedical demonstrations, generated hypotheses have been connected to subsequent experimental validation. These results justify philosophical attention because the old boundary between idea and execution is already porous.

They do not justify the claim that science has been fully automated. Existing systems depend heavily on human-defined objectives, available literature, chosen tools, datasets, laboratory interfaces, and evaluation functions. Their successes are concentrated in environments where the relevant operations can be digitized and where feedback is available at tolerable cost.

Co-Scientist is instructive because its architecture resembles an internal scientific community. Agents generate proposals, debate, rank, and refine them. The system can produce hypotheses that human researchers regard as useful and, in some cases, empirically promising. But it still relies on human problem framing and scientific context. The result is better understood as a new kind of collective cognitive instrument than as proof that scientific institutions can be removed.

Robin moves closer to experimental biology by coupling literature, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. The AI Scientist shows that a substantial machine-learning research loop can be automated, from idea generation through code and manuscript production. ERA demonstrates the power of automated search over empirical software when a quality metric is available. Each system reveals the same structural fact: once an evaluator can be executed cheaply, generation can be scaled aggressively.

This leads to a basic law of automated research: the generator can become stronger than the judge. If agents produce hypotheses, code, or models faster than they can be tested against a trustworthy criterion, output accumulates faster than knowledge. The bottleneck moves from creation to discrimination.

Domains with cheap evaluators will therefore automate first. Mathematical proofs with formal verifiers, software benchmarks, certain simulations, and highly standardized laboratory tasks provide feedback that agents can use directly. Problems involving ambiguous objectives, sparse data, tacit experimental knowledge, long causal chains, or contested values are harder because the evaluation function is itself

part of the scientific problem.

The deepest limitation is not “lack of creativity.” AI systems can generate surprising combinations and candidate explanations. Nor is it simply lack of language ability. The difficult issue is pursuitworthiness: deciding which problem, anomaly, or hypothesis deserves scarce access to experiments, instruments, experts, and social attention.

Human researchers are not infallible at this either. Scientific history is full of fashionable dead ends and neglected anomalies. The difference is that automation can scale the error. A biased human selection process may distort a field; a globally deployed selection model can synchronize the distortion across institutions.

Tacit knowledge presents another challenge. Published articles are sanitized traces of research. They contain far less information about failed protocols, fragile tricks, laboratory skill, ambiguous observations, and local judgment than researchers actually use. AI trained mainly on successful literature receives a biased view of the scientific process.

This is why early systems should be interpreted as probes into the architecture of science rather than as replacements for scientists. They reveal which parts of research were already sufficiently formalized to be automated and which parts depend on unarticulated evaluators, access to resistant reality, or institutional judgment.

The appropriate response is neither denial nor technological triumphalism. To say “AI cannot really do science because humans still define the problem” simply moves the boundary whenever automation advances. To say “AI has already become a scientist because it can produce papers” confuses scientific artifacts with scientific institutions.

A more stable criterion is agent-neutral. If a human or machine can generate a model, expose it to independent resistance, preserve the evidence of failure, revise appropriately, and participate in a community of criticism, then it participates in science. If a human produces polished outputs in a closed loop that cannot learn from defeat, biological authorship does not rescue the process.

The philosophical importance of AI is therefore that it forces science to define itself without appealing to the human identity of the scientist. What matters is the architecture through which claims become answerable to something they do not control.

The evidence available in 2026 should nevertheless be read conservatively. Demonstrations in machine learning and biomedical research occur in domains with unusually rich digital traces and accessible evaluators. Successful automation of those loops does not establish that the same architectures can choose worthwhile problems in fields with slow feedback, tacit laboratory practice, contested concepts, or expensive real-world experiments. The proper conclusion is not universal autonomy but a rapidly expanding boundary of what can be delegated.

This caution is philosophically useful because it separates two questions that publicity often merges. One asks whether AI can perform more stages of research; the answer is increasingly yes. The other asks whether an automated system can sustain an open-ended research program whose objectives, representations, and evaluators may themselves need revision. The second is a much stronger requirement and remains an empirical research question rather than a settled fact.

When Variety of Results Conceals a Narrowing of the Space

AI appears to maximize diversity because it can generate enormous numbers of outputs. This can be misleading. Diversity of surface variants is not the same as diversity of conceptual coordinates. A million models can differ while sharing the same ontology, objective function, dataset, benchmark, and assumptions about what counts as success.

This distinction can be described as the difference between volume and dimensionality. Volume is the number of explored points. Dimensionality concerns the number of substantively independent directions in which the search can move. Automated systems can increase volume dramatically while leaving dimensionality nearly unchanged.

The 2026 observational evidence associating AI use with individual productivity gains and collective narrowing is therefore philosophically important even if causal conclusions remain uncertain. It suggests a plausible institutional mechanism: researchers use AI most effectively in domains rich in data, mature literature, and established evaluators; those domains then become even more productive and attractive, pulling attention away from poorly formalized regions.

This is a classic positive-feedback loop. Data-rich topics support better models. Better models increase output. Higher output generates more citations, datasets, and benchmarks. The resulting infrastructure makes the topic still easier to automate. Fields with sparse data, disputed categories, or difficult experiments fall further behind in apparent productivity.

The effect can be rational at every local decision. A researcher chooses a tractable problem. A funder chooses a proposal with measurable progress. A model recommends literature similar to successful prior work. A journal accepts a paper with a clear benchmark improvement. No actor intends monoculture, yet the system converges.

Automated recommendation can intensify the convergence. If literature discovery, collaborator matching, hypothesis suggestion, and funding triage all use related models, the same latent representation begins to organize multiple stages of science. Ideas far from the learned manifold may become less visible precisely because the system is optimized for relevance.

This is an epistemic version of algorithmic filter bubbles, but the stakes are different. A personal media bubble affects what a person sees. An epistemic monoculture affects what civilization bothers to test. The danger is not only ideological agreement; it is loss of unexplored dimensions.

Benchmarks create a particularly strong selection pressure. They are useful because they allow comparison and cumulative progress. But once a benchmark becomes a central currency of prestige, the field begins optimizing for it. Improvements can become real and important while the relation between benchmark and underlying goal gradually weakens.

AI accelerates this process because local search becomes cheap. The system can explore thousands of architecture changes, prompts, training procedures, and hyperparameters. If the evaluator is fixed, that search becomes extraordinarily efficient. The scientific question then moves upstream: is the evaluator measuring what matters, and what alternatives disappear because they perform poorly under the current metric?

Monoculture also appears through foundation models. Multiple agents may look independent while sharing training data, architectures, or cultural assumptions. Agreement among them is then weaker evidence than it appears. Scientific pluralism requires diversity of error, not merely diversity of prompts or personas.

The same issue affects synthetic data. Synthetic datasets can expand coverage and protect privacy, but if models are increasingly trained and evaluated on data produced by related models, the ecosystem can become self-referential. Errors and omissions may stabilize as conventions rather than being corrected by new contact with the world.

The answer is not to forbid shared infrastructure. Standardization is one source of scientific power. It makes results comparable and reproducible. The challenge is to maintain deliberate channels of heterogeneity: alternative datasets, independent instruments, competing ontologies, different model families, human field observations, and experiments that do not share the same generative assumptions.

Funding portfolios should therefore be audited for common dependencies. A hundred projects with different titles may be one epistemic bet if they all rely on the same corpus, assay, benchmark, foundation model, or causal structure. Portfolio diversity must be measured in assumptions and failure modes, not only in topics and institutions.

AI can help perform this audit by mapping conceptual similarity, shared evidence, and model genealogies. But the evaluator of diversity must itself be plural. A single embedding model cannot be allowed to define the only geometry of novelty.

Automated epistemic monoculture is not a future with no results. It may be a future with unprecedented result production. Stagnation would take the form of an avalanche of successful local changes while the coordinates of inquiry become increasingly difficult to escape.

A practical warning follows for evaluation systems that estimate novelty through semantic distance. Distance in an embedding space can detect repetition and support literature search, but it inherits the representation used to build that space. A genuinely new ontology may initially look incoherent rather than distant in the right direction. Novelty assessment should therefore combine similarity measures with explicit examination of what entities, relations, observables, and interventions a proposal makes possible.

The Agent Does Not Matter; the Architecture of Criticism Does

Discussion of AI in science is often organized around whether the machine “understands.” The question is philosophically important, but it can obscure the institutional problem. Human science is not credible because every researcher perfectly understands every mechanism. It is credible when claims enter an architecture in which they can be criticized, reproduced, compared, and corrected.

A human can rationalize, forget, protect favored beliefs, and remain opaque even to himself. An AI system can be more traceable in some respects because it can preserve logs, versions, and executable histories. Conversely, a large model can contain representations difficult to interpret, while a provider may control access to weights, training data, and interfaces. Neither biological nor artificial origin confers automatic epistemic superiority.

The criterion must therefore move from agent to system. Who frames the problem? What data are accessible? How are hypotheses selected? Is there separation between generator and evaluator? What tests would reveal error? Who can audit the result? What happens after failure? These questions describe scientific quality more reliably than abstract debate over machine consciousness.

The architecture of criticism must begin with provenance. Every claim should be linked to the sources, data, transformations, code, and decisions that produced it. When an agent reformulates a research question, the difference between the original and operational formulation should be visible. When code changes, the reason and effect should remain reconstructible. Without such memory, automation produces results that cannot be assigned to a verifiable path.

For AI systems, four minimal infrastructures follow. The first is a versioned registry of generated hypotheses, including rejected variants, so selection itself can be audited. The second is executable provenance for data, code, models, prompts, tools, and decisions. The third is plurality of evaluators: simulation, formal proof, holdout data, physical experiment, and independent human or algorithmic criticism should provide error modes that are not identical. The fourth is accountability: an identifiable actor or institution must remain responsible for objectives, limits, and the response to failure. “The agent decided” cannot terminate the normative chain.

Independence of evaluation is crucial. Absolute independence is impossible, but dependencies can be mapped. If generator and critic use the same model, same data, and same objective, their agreement has limited evidential value. A formal solver, physical experiment, independently collected dataset, or external team introduces a different form of resistance.

The architecture should also preserve multiple hypotheses long enough. Ranking systems tend to converge rapidly and delete low-scoring branches. In fundamental research, some branches should remain available because the current evaluator may be incomplete. An archive is not passive storage; it is a reservoir of options that can be revisited after new data, instruments, or theories appear.

Automated criticism must be adversarial rather than stylistic. A useful critic searches for conditions under which the conclusion fails, competing explanations of the same evidence, minimal changes of assumptions that reverse the verdict, and hidden dependencies between training and evaluation. A review that summarizes strengths and weaknesses without constructing discriminating tests reproduces the appearance of peer review rather than its deepest epistemic function.

Human appeal remains necessary, not because humans are infallible but because technical systems can concentrate power. Automated systems involved in funding, publication, or research prioritization should be contestable. The reasons for decisions should be inspectable enough that researchers can introduce alternatives and request evaluation of hypotheses rejected by the automated filter.

Human oversight, however, must not become a mechanism for restoring pedigree. A committee should not be able to overturn a robust automated finding merely because it threatens a powerful center. Governance must audit both directions: machine bias and human capture.

The strongest architecture is adversarial collaboration among different forms of intelligence and validation. Humans contribute context, values, tacit knowledge, and sensitivity to poorly formalized phenomena. Agents can search large spaces, preserve memory, compare alternatives, and detect inconsistency. Formal systems and physical instruments provide forms of resistance that neither humans nor language models can negotiate away.

In this architecture, AI is neither servant nor sovereign. It is a participant in an institution of correctability. Its scientific status does not depend on imitating a human researcher but on entering a circuit in which claims have consequences, errors can be localized, and results alter subsequent policy.

This agent-neutrality also has legal and ethical consequences. Responsibility cannot be transferred to a system merely because it generated the hypothesis. The institution that defined the objective, granted laboratory access, and published the result remains responsible for the process. At the same time, intellectual attribution should become more granular: who framed the objective, generated the alternative, built the test, interpreted the result, and authorized intervention?

A single authorship label will increasingly describe distributed research poorly. Provenance of contribution will matter not only for credit but for locating error. The same infrastructure that tells us who deserves recognition should tell us where a failed assumption entered the chain.

The credible future is therefore not the laboratory without humans. It is a constitutional architecture in which human and artificial agents can criticize one another’s frames while the world remains an arbiter that neither side can completely simulate.

9.5 Human Command, Responsibility, Credit, and Benefit

Human command should not be confused with the requirement that a person click approve at the end of an automated process. Command exists only when people or legitimate institutions retain meaningful authority over purpose, constraints, irreversible actions, release, and the distribution of consequences. They must receive evidence that is adequate for the decision, possess enough time and competence to interpret it, be able to stop or redirect the process, and have a path for appeal. A nominal human in the loop who cannot reconstruct how a claim was produced or alter the system's course is a liability holder, not a commander.

A Constitution of Decision Rights

Scientific automation requires a constitution because different actions carry different kinds of authority. An agent may be allowed to search literature, generate code in a sandbox, or propose experiments without permission for every step. It should not automatically be allowed to purchase materials, expose research subjects, change a clinical protocol, publish a high-consequence claim, or deploy a technology. Decision rights can be attached to action classes, resource thresholds, risk profiles, evidence states, and named institutional roles. The constitutional layer should be inspectable and versioned, so that a change in authority is itself an event in the research record.

This architecture should support delegation without pretending that every decision can be anticipated. When a process encounters a novel action or a conflict among rules, it must abstain and escalate. Escalation should include the relevant claim-evidence path, uncertainties, alternatives, expected consequences, and the reason the existing policy is insufficient. The research problem is to determine whether such evidence packages genuinely improve human judgment or merely overwhelm reviewers with machine-produced detail. Interfaces should therefore be evaluated through decision quality, reconstruction time, missed harms, and the ability of decision-makers to identify when the system framed the problem incorrectly.

The Researcher as Architect of Correctability

As implementation, search, and routine analysis become cheaper, the researcher's contribution shifts toward the architecture of inquiry. This includes deciding which uncertainty matters, choosing or inventing representations, identifying sources of independent resistance, designing evaluators that cannot be satisfied by superficial optimization, and determining which consequences require public or specialist authorization. These are not uniquely human capacities in principle. They are the capacities that remain scarce when local generation and execution are abundant, regardless of whether they are eventually exercised by people, machines, or mixed institutions.

Coding agents make this shift visible. A small team can create a prototype that would once have required a large implementation effort. The resulting temptation is to treat fluent implementation as evidence that the underlying research question has been clarified. In fact, faster implementation increases the cost of conceptual negligence. The researcher must specify invariants, test boundaries, provenance, threat models, data rights, fallback behavior, and conditions of abandonment before the first successful demonstration becomes the de facto architecture. Books, design arguments, executable specifications, adversarial examples, and early prototypes become complementary instruments of preparation.

The role should also retain direct contact with failure. Excessive delegation can deskill researchers until they can no longer distinguish a surprising result from a broken pipeline or a plausible mechanism from an artefact of the evaluator. Critical nodes therefore need deliberate human practice: inspecting raw measurements, reproducing selected analyses independently, challenging model assumptions, and conducting periodic manual or alternative-tool audits. The objective is not nostalgia for manual work. It is to preserve enough competence for oversight to remain substantive.

Credit, Responsibility, and Benefit

A single authorship label will increasingly misrepresent distributed research. Contributions may include problem framing, data creation, instrument operation, model design, code generation, experimental execution, criticism, replication, compliance review, community participation, and decisions that prevented an unsafe release. A research object should record these contributions without implying that all are equivalent. It should also preserve responsibility: who authorized an action, who controlled the model or data, who could have stopped the process, and who had access to the evidence required for the decision.

Human command must also include the distribution of benefit. Automated science can concentrate returns in the owners of models, compute, data, laboratories, and validation infrastructure while externalizing risk to subjects, workers, public institutions, and communities that supplied the data. A research object should therefore preserve not only technical contribution but claims about authorship, data rights, community participation, licensing, public value, and responsibility. Benefit-sharing will remain a political choice, but infrastructure can make the choice explicit and contestable rather than allowing the default ownership stack to decide it invisibly.

This requirement is not a demand that software determine justice. It is a demand that the system stop erasing the information needed for a political and ethical decision. Data-use conditions, community agreements, public funding, intellectual-property assignments, environmental cost, and downstream revenue can be linked to the same project history that records scientific contributions. Different institutions may choose different benefit rules, but the decision should not be made accidentally by whichever contract or platform happens to own the final artefact.

A Human-AI Republic, Not a Ceremonial Monarchy

The most credible institutional model is a republic of heterogeneous powers rather than a sovereign artificial scientist supervised by a ceremonial human monarch. Generators, critics, formal kernels, laboratories, archives, compliance systems, domain experts, affected communities, and release authorities should constrain one another. No actor should possess an unrestricted path from idea to consequence. The system remains capable of fast local action, but consequential transitions require evidence states and decision rights that can be contested.

Human command does not imply that people must always have the final epistemic answer. A machine may discover a representation, proof, or mechanism that no person could have generated. The relevant question is whether the path from claim to consequence remains correctable and legitimate. Humans may authorize experiments because they bear responsibility for subjects and resources, while formal kernels decide proof validity and instruments provide empirical resistance. Authority is distributed according to the kind of judgment, not reserved wholesale for biological agents.

A practical research project could build a constitutional sandbox for an AI-assisted programme. It would encode action classes and decision rights, simulate conflicts and novel cases, measure when escalation occurs, and compare human decisions with and without structured evidence packages. A second study could examine whether contribution and benefit records change negotiation among researchers, data providers, and communities. A third could test whether periodic independent manual audits preserve competence and detect errors missed by automated critics. The programme should reject its human-command design if authority becomes ceremonial, if escalation is so frequent that delegation collapses, or if the system concentrates effective power in the owner of the orchestration platform.

The objective is therefore neither maximum autonomy nor permanent human micromanagement. It is maximum responsible delegation compatible with plural inquiry, independent resistance, human welfare, and legitimate control of consequence. Machines should search more broadly, execute more reliably, preserve more memory, and expose more error. People should remain able to choose purposes, challenge representations, decide what risks are acceptable, stop the process, and share in the benefits. A scientific system that automates discovery while removing those capabilities would be technologically impressive and institutionally regressive.

Chapter 10. From Principles to Technology Concepts: The Research Portfolio

The final chapter converts the preceding arguments into a portfolio of researchable technology families. The objective is not to freeze a product architecture. It is to state the missing layer, the scientific reason for believing that the layer matters, the artefact that could embody the idea, the relations to neighbouring components, the evaluator regime, and the observations that would

force revision. The programme should be judged by whether these formulations make future

projects more precise and falsifiable, not by whether every proposed name survives

implementation.

10.1 Research Objects, Specifications, Memory, Novelty, and Relevance

The first family of projects concerns the scientific object itself. Contemporary research is still organised around papers, repositories, notebooks, and databases that expose fragments of an inquiry but not the semantic trajectory by which claims changed. The research question is whether a durable, evidence-bearing object can make scientific correction computationally tractable without pretending that every concept is already formal. The work is not primarily a new file format. It is the construction of a layer in which claims, evidence, reasons, negative results, uncertainty, and decisions can be linked, versioned, queried, and selectively recomputed.

Project direction Core question and possible demonstrator

Evidence-Bearing Research Demonstrate a versioned object linking specifications, claims, evidence, negative results,

Objectcriticism, provenance, and decisions; test whether independent reviewers reconstruct claim history more accurately than from papers and repositories alone.
Epistemic Version ControlDevelop semantic commits, branches, merges, and diffs for scientific meaning; falsify the

approach if domain experts cannot reliably agree that the generated diffs capture consequential changes.

Living Specification Compiler Translate a research intention into rival hypotheses, controls, budgets, stop conditions, and evidence obligations while preserving ambiguity that should not yet be formalized.

Validity Dossier Generator Build layered, inspectable release packages for computational and experimental work; compare review time, error detection, and replication outcomes with conventional supplementary material.

The central hypothesis is that a scientific project can be represented at a level between raw event logging and retrospective narrative. The object must preserve claims, assumptions, evidence, objections, negative branches, environments, and decisions without requiring every domain to accept one exhaustive ontology. A small common kernel may describe identity, provenance, scope, support, opposition, dependency, uncertainty, and authority. Domain extensions can then represent a proof obligation, a laboratory calibration, a clinical endpoint, a qualitative coding decision, or a model-selection event. The research challenge is to discover whether this layered representation remains coherent when the same claim moves among disciplines and forms of evidence.

The object should be evidence-bearing rather than merely metadata-rich. A claim is not useful because it has many fields, but because an inspector can follow why it was introduced, what supports it, what would oppose it, which transformations produced the current formulation, and what downstream conclusions depend on it. This creates a different design objective from the ordinary knowledge graph. The graph must preserve contestability and versioned reasons, not only relations that appear settled. Contradictions, alternative operationalizations, and unresolved status are first-class states rather than errors to be normalized away.

Epistemic version control should distinguish a textual edit from a scientific change. Rephrasing a paragraph may leave the claim invariant, while changing an inclusion criterion, causal assumption, measurement procedure, or evaluator can alter the meaning of every downstream result. A semantic commit should therefore identify the type of change, the evidence or decision that motivated it, and the branches that require reconsideration. The system may use language models to propose a diff, but acceptance requires domain-aware validation and the ability to display uncertainty when several interpretations remain plausible.

The living specification is the forward-looking counterpart of the semantic history. It records the question, rival hypotheses, admissible claims, controls, evidence obligations, budgets, stop conditions, safety constraints, and decision rights that currently govern the inquiry. It must remain revisable because research changes its own problem. The compiler is not expected to turn natural-language intent into a complete formal program. Its purpose is to expose missing commitments, produce candidate executable fragments, and preserve the relationship between the original intention and the actions later performed. an executable research representation, dynamic circuits, or a governed interpretation runtime may provide implementation experiments for this layer, but the hypothesis is independent of those technologies.

A useful first demonstrator would follow one computational project from initial question to publication and independent rerun. The same project would be represented conventionally and as an evidence-bearing object. Reviewers would receive either the paper and repository or a claim-centred interface containing semantic diffs, negative branches, environment capture, and provenance. The research question is not whether the richer interface feels impressive. It is whether it changes error discovery, reconstruction time, reviewer agreement, and the ability to explain why a claim changed.

The difficult issue is granularity. If every action becomes a provenance event, the object becomes unusable. If only final artefacts are preserved, the object reproduces the paper's compression. Research must identify which transitions are epistemically consequential and how this differs across domains. A semantic commit in a clinical study is not the same as one in theorem proving. The common layer may need a small vocabulary of claim transitions combined with domain-specific extensions.

Evaluation should include adversarial reconstruction. Independent teams can receive partial objects with selected provenance removed, contradictory branches inserted, or semantic changes obscured. The system succeeds only if inspectors can localize what is missing and if the representation improves their ability to detect consequential change compared with ordinary papers, notebooks, and repositories. It should fail visibly when experts cannot agree on the proposed semantic diff or when the cost of maintaining the object exceeds the value of the correction it enables.

A second line of work concerns interoperability. Research objects should exchange claims and evidence without forcing laboratories to reveal protected data or replace mature domain systems. This suggests content-addressed artefacts, portable provenance envelopes, typed references to external evidence, and controlled views for different audiences. The project should test whether a workbench can recompute only the branches affected by a change and whether another implementation can verify the same dependency path. If the object functions only inside one orchestration platform, it has reproduced the lock-in that the programme intends to avoid.

Representation and memory form one project family because a novelty system cannot be stronger than the record against which it compares a candidate. The relevant demonstrators must therefore test the research object, the idea representation, retrieval, lineage, and temporal evaluation together as well as separately.

The second family concerns the representation and search of scientific ideas. Retrieval systems rank documents, while scientific reasoning compares mechanisms, assumptions, transformations, and failures that cut across documents. A research programme must therefore investigate operational representations that remain plural and evidence-grounded. The objective is not an oracle that certifies originality. It is an inspectable system that can show what a candidate inherits, which precedents were searched, which transformations were allowed, where a reconstruction fails, and how stable the residual is under alternative corpora and representations.

Project directionCore question and possible demonstrator
Operational-Idea AtlasRepresent multiple decompositions and typed identity relations across literature; evaluate

through blinded novelty, precedent, and synthesis tasks against search, RAG, and citation-graph baselines.

Novelty Residual Engine Test whether structured reconstruction residuals using symbolic, geometric, or high-dimensional representations predict expert-judged novelty better than semantic distance alone.

Project direction Core question and possible demonstrator

Relevance-Before-Reasoning Retrieve evidence likely to become relevant in later reasoning even when its role is not yet

Retrievalknown, while suppressing keyword coincidences and documenting why each item entered the candidate set.
Project ConsciousnessMaintain cross-agent memory of decisions, abandoned branches, unresolved anomalies,

and forgotten evidence; test whether it revives useful alternatives and reduces repeated dead ends.

Ordinary retrieval asks which documents are similar to a query. Scientific search often requires evidence whose future role is not yet known. A mechanism described in another field, a failed experiment with different terminology, or an old measurement anomaly may become relevant only after several reasoning steps. The research objective is therefore to retrieve candidate evidence with plausible structural relevance while suppressing superficial keyword overlap. A system should be able to explain which mechanism, assumption, transformation, contradiction, or methodological role caused an item to enter the candidate set, even when it cannot yet explain the complete path to the final conclusion.

This layer should be tested against strong document RAG, dense retrieval, citation graphs, and human search rather than against weak keyword baselines. Evaluation can ask whether the system finds evidence later judged useful in a blind reasoning task, whether it increases the diversity of live hypotheses without overwhelming the user, and whether its explanations remain stable under changes of wording. A useful abstention state is essential. When the representation does not support a relevance judgment, the system should return uncertainty and alternative search strategies rather than manufacture a causal story for its ranking.

An operational-idea atlas should not reduce an idea to a document embedding. It can represent goals, mechanisms, assumptions, entities, transformations, constraints, expected observations, and relations to earlier work. The same scientific contribution may require several decompositions because a chemist, a statistician, and a historian of science can identify different units of novelty. The project should therefore maintain plural views linked to source spans and allow disagreements over identity to persist. The output is not a global same-as relation but an inspectable account of what is inherited, transformed, recombined, or left unexplained under each representation.

Candidate technologies include structured semantic parsing, claim and mechanism graphs, natural-logic relations, causal models, high-dimensional symbolic representations, geometric cones, and learned proposal models. Their value should be tested through ablation and disagreement, not through architectural elegance. A distributed novelty residual is useful only if the reconstruction and the residual remain meaningful across corpora, languages, disciplines, and decomposition choices. A learned model may propose analogies, while symbolic constraints check role consistency and provenance. No representation should be promoted to a universal ontology merely because it performs well on one historical benchmark.

This project family should be evaluated by temporal backtesting and real research tasks rather than by synthetic similarity labels alone. A system can be given only the literature available before a historical cutoff and asked to identify relevant antecedents, open contradictions, or unusual combinations later recognized by a field. It can also support live teams whose members are blinded to whether they use ordinary search, document RAG, citation graphs, or an operational-idea atlas. The key outcomes are not only final novelty judgments, but the quality of evidence retrieved, the diversity of hypotheses considered, and the frequency with which the system reveals that its own representation is inadequate.

Scientific memory should preserve reasons for abandonment. An idea rejected because a reagent was unavailable is different from one rejected by a decisive experiment. A branch that failed under one operationalization may become relevant when another representation appears. Project consciousness should therefore not be a conversational memory that accumulates summaries. It should be a structured history of decisions, assumptions, contradictions, and unresolved status, with mechanisms for forgetting low-value detail while retaining the conditions under which a forgotten branch might deserve revival.

Memory needs retrieval policies as much as storage. A project consciousness can reactivate a branch when its rejection condition has changed, when a new instrument makes an old test possible, or when another domain introduces a compatible mechanism. It should not continually resurface every abandoned idea. Research is needed on forgetting, relevance thresholds, causal links between decisions and evidence, and the representation of unresolved status. The benchmark is whether teams avoid repeated dead ends and recover valuable alternatives without suffering a larger burden of archival noise and false analogy.

This family should also study the ecology of idea portfolios. If all candidates are ranked by the same novelty score, the atlas becomes another mechanism of convergence. Portfolio managers can preserve alternatives with different mechanisms, evidence dependencies, and representations, allocating small exploratory budgets before demanding direct performance. The approach should be rejected if diversity becomes random accumulation or if option value cannot be distinguished from the strategic relabeling of weak ideas. The atlas earns a role only when it improves later reasoning, discovery, or correction under blind comparison.

10.2 Corrective, Experimental, Formal, and Governance Infrastructure

The third family concerns criticism as infrastructure. Generation scales readily because one model can propose many candidates. Scientific resistance does not scale in the same way. Independent reproduction, causal challenge, specialist judgment, privacy review, copyright analysis, and ethical authorization require heterogeneous evidence and often different institutions. The central technical question is how to turn criticism from free-form commentary into typed, dependency-aware evidence without reducing judgment to a universal score.

Project directionCore question and possible demonstrator
Independent Critic NetworkCreate critics with distinct evidence sources, tools, model families, and authority; measure

whether dependency fingerprints predict correlated failure better than agent count or stated persona.

Severe-Test Design Agent Generate experiments targeted at named error modes and compare their information gain with conventional confirmatory proposals.

Automated Peer Review and Coordinate claim-specific reviewers, reproducibility checks, novelty analysis, rebuttal, and

Rebuttalhuman adjudication; evaluate error discovery, fairness, calibration, and reviewer effort.
Configurablea Interpret project-specific legal, ethical, copyright, contractual, privacy, and institutional

rules; require source-linked explanations and abstention when rules conflict or facts are

configurable research-compliance assistantmissing.
Controlled Data-Use AgentMediate access to sensitive data, privacy-preserving computation, lineage, minimization,

and purpose limitation; compare enforcement and usability across federated, synthetic, encrypted, and trusted-execution approaches.

A critic should be defined by the property it challenges and the evidence it can obtain, not by a theatrical persona. One critic may test statistical calibration, another reproduce an execution environment, another search for causal alternatives, and another inspect whether a claim exceeds the scope of its data. Their outputs should identify the target claim, the error mode, the procedure used, the result, the dependency fingerprint, and the consequence for the evidence state. Free-form prose can accompany the result, but it should not be the only artefact returned to the workbench.

The critic network should include deterministic checks, formal tools, independently implemented pipelines, specialist humans, and agents based on different models or corpora. Multiple prompts to the same foundation model do not create meaningful independence.
