Research should estimate correlated error by changing dependencies deliberately and observing which failures move together. A dependency fingerprint may include training lineage, retrieval source, code base, laboratory, operator, statistical library, instrument, funding interest, and institutional role. The goal is not an impossible proof of independence, but a decision-relevant account of shared vulnerability.

A severe-test agent begins from a named error that matters. It searches for an observation, intervention, counterexample, or replication design that would probably expose that error if it existed. This differs from asking for another experiment likely to produce a publishable effect. The agent must estimate what alternatives the test discriminates, what auxiliary assumptions it relies on, and what result would remain ambiguous. In formal domains, the severe test may be a counterexample search or independent proof. In empirical domains, it may be a holdout population, negative control, alternative instrument, or intervention that separates rival mechanisms.

Automated peer review should orchestrate these critics rather than imitate a conventional report. A claim-specific review graph can show which parts were checked, which remain unexamined, where critics disagree, and what evidence a rebuttal adds. Reviewers and authors should be able to challenge the critic's method and dependency, not merely its language. The system should preserve minority reports and the history of revisions so that later replication can revisit an unresolved objection. A single acceptance score would destroy much of the value created by this richer process.

Compliance is not an administrative appendix when it determines which data may be used, which experiments may be performed, and which results may be released. A configurable copilot can represent legal, ethical, copyright, contractual, and institutional rules together with their sources, jurisdiction, scope, conflicts, and required authority. Its output should distinguish clear prohibitions, conditional permissions, missing facts, and questions that require human interpretation. It should never convert regulatory ambiguity into a false scientific certainty.

The controlled-data agent applies these constraints to actual data flows. It can enforce purpose limitation, minimization, access conditions, retention, lineage, and privacy-preserving computation. Related approaches include federated learning, secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, trusted execution environments, synthetic data, and controlled analysis enclaves. The a privacy-governed data-use agent is one possible ScriptaHub implementation line. The research issue is not choosing a fashionable privacy technology, but determining whether the resulting evidence remains valid, auditable, and usable under the protection mechanism.

A promising integrated demonstrator is an automated validity dossier for an AI-assisted study. Generator agents produce candidate analyses, but independent critics use different retrieval services, execution environments, statistical tests, and model families. Their dependency fingerprints are visible. A peer-review orchestrator asks claim-specific questions, a compliance copilot checks the configured rules, and a controlled-data agent verifies purpose, minimization, and access. Human reviewers see disagreements and missing evidence rather than a single confidence score.

The programme should expect abstention. Law and ethics contain conflicts, exceptions, and jurisdictional variation; privacy depends on data flows and context; peer review depends on expert judgment. A trustworthy agent must be able to say which rule it applied, which facts it lacks, and which authority must decide. The central benchmark is therefore not automated agreement with a reference answer alone. It includes calibration, source fidelity, error severity, the detection of conflicts, robustness to changed rules, and the quality of escalation to human decision-makers.

Evaluation should include planted errors, disputed rules, hidden dependencies, inaccessible evidence, and deliberately misleading consensus. The system should be penalized for confident but unsupported closure more heavily than for justified abstention. Human reviewers should be compared with and without the dossier, and downstream replications should test whether the identified weaknesses predicted actual failure. The project should be revised if structured criticism adds bureaucracy without increasing error discovery, if dependence mapping proves too coarse to guide action, or if compliance agents encourage institutions to outsource responsibility to an interface.

Corrective infrastructure and experimental automation form a second family. A generator, laboratory, formal solver, or simulator becomes scientific only when its claims enter a system of independent tests, policy constraints, replication, uncertainty, and review proportionate to the domain.

The fourth family concerns the transition from language to action. Automated science becomes consequential when a hypothesis can allocate compute, modify code, order a simulation, control an instrument, or alter a protocol. The relevant projects must connect specifications to active learning, formal methods, laboratory control, and domain-sensitive safety. Their success depends less on agent fluency than on evaluator strength, calibration, provenance, and the ability to stop when the world no longer matches the model.

Project directionCore question and possible demonstrator
Portfolio Diversity ManagerAllocate budgets across rival hypotheses and representations using information gain and

diversity rather than one performance metric; test resistance to premature convergence and Goodhart effects.

Project directionCore question and possible demonstrator
AutonomousExperiment Link a living specification to simulation or laboratory actions under safety envelopes,
Connectorcalibration rules, telemetry, and rollback; start in domains with strong evaluators and low consequence.

Formal Discovery Workbench Combine conjecture generation, code synthesis, symbolic regression, counterexample search, model checking, and proof kernels; distinguish proof of a formal statement from adequacy of the formalization.

The safest starting points are domains with comparatively strong evaluators and reversible actions. Computational experiments, formal proofs, model checking, symbolic regression, and instrument simulators allow rapid iteration and clear traces. The programme can then move toward physical laboratories with standardized equipment, well-defined safety envelopes, and independent measurement. Clinical, social, and high-consequence settings require slower validation, more plural evidence, and stronger institutional authority.

This ordering is epistemic rather than a declaration that formal sciences are simple. A proof assistant can verify a derivation only relative to a formal statement and trusted kernel. A test suite can certify behavior only over the cases it represents. A simulation can be executed exactly while modeling the wrong system. Strong evaluators make local automation possible, but the programme must preserve the distinction between success inside the representation and adequacy of the representation itself. The interface between formal and empirical resistance is therefore a major research boundary.

Active learning, Bayesian optimization, value-of-information analysis, causal design, and quality-diversity search can help choose the next experiment. The agent should state what uncertainty or rivalry the action is intended to reduce, what cost and risk it carries, and how its value depends on the current model. A portfolio manager can allocate small budgets to alternative representations and controls rather than sending all resources toward the candidate with the highest estimated reward. This is especially important when the evaluator is uncertain or the search landscape contains deceptive local optima.

Every closed loop should be tested for seduction by its evaluator. Active learning can find the region that most improves a model while ignoring the region that matters scientifically. A robotic laboratory can optimize a proxy measurement while calibration drifts. A proof system can certify a statement whose formalization misses the intended theorem. Demonstrators should therefore include adversarial evaluators, holdout instruments, alternative operationalizations, and periodic human review of the objective itself. The goal is not merely autonomous execution, but the ability to detect when the loop is efficiently solving the wrong problem.

Autonomous-laboratory connectors should translate a living specification into bounded instrument actions, calibration events, sample identities, telemetry, and evidence records. The connector is not merely an API wrapper. It enforces a safety envelope, confirms that the physical configuration matches the assumed state, records deviations, and prevents an agent from treating a failed instrument command as a scientific observation. The same specification should be executable first against a simulator or digital twin, then against controlled hardware, with explicit evidence about where the surrogate ceases to predict the instrument.

A laboratory demonstrator can focus on one narrow closed loop with mature instrumentation. It should compare human-designed and agent-designed experiments, use an independent measurement channel, introduce calibration drift and sample-label errors, and test whether the system detects the mismatch before promoting a claim. Success is not the number of experiments per day. It is the increase in informative experiments per unit of cost and risk while preserving traceability and the ability to stop. A faster loop that amplifies systematic error is a negative result, not progress.

Domain rigor profiles express what kinds of evidence, reversibility, latency, uncertainty, and authority apply to a field. Mathematics may require a trusted proof kernel and inspection of the formalization. Software research may rely on tests, static analysis, performance measurements, and reproducible environments. Chemistry may require calibration, sample lineage, physical controls, and hazard constraints. Clinical and social research add consent, population transport, delayed outcomes, institutional effects, and contested values. Interpretive inquiry may depend on plural readings and source criticism that should not be collapsed into a single optimization target.

The research question is whether a common workbench can host these profiles without imposing one method. Shared layers may include provenance, decision rights, evidence states, uncertainty, and versioning. The evaluators and admissible actions remain domain-specific. Transfer should occur through explicit mappings rather than analogy by rhetoric. The programme should reject a generic automation layer when its abstractions hide the very differences that determine scientific validity or ethical legitimacy.

10.3 Institutional Design, Human Command, Integrated Demonstrators, and Revision

The fifth family concerns science as a social and political system. Pedigree, visibility, networks, capital, institutional authority, and platform ownership influence which questions receive attention and which failures remain visible. These forces cannot be eliminated by an algorithm, and expertise should not be flattened into anonymous voting. The research challenge is to design counterweights: blinded evaluation where appropriate, conflict and dependency graphs, protected exploratory portfolios, publication of informative failure, rights of appeal, plural funding mechanisms, and governance that keeps humans in command of consequence while allowing machines substantial local autonomy.

Project direction Core question and possible demonstrator

Pedigree and Power Quantify the influence of institution, network, geography, funding, and platform ownership

Observatoryon attention and evaluation while designing mitigations that preserve legitimate expertise.
Anti-Monoculture AuditMeasure concentration of topics, datasets, citations, ontologies, evaluators, and model

families in AI-assisted science; test interventions that preserve plural search spaces.

Credit and Benefit Ledger Represent contributions by researchers, critics, agents, datasets, instruments, and communities, and study rules for attribution, licensing, revenue, and public benefit that remain open to appeal.

Human-Command Constitution Define decision rights by capability, consequence, domain, and evidence; test whether users can genuinely stop, revise, and understand consequential automated processes rather than merely approve them ceremonially.

A pedigree-and-power audit should show how attention, funding, review, infrastructure, and model access are distributed. It can combine citation and collaboration networks with grant histories, institutional affiliation, geography, ownership, data access, model dependencies, and reviewer relations. The purpose is not to calculate a moral ranking of institutions or individuals. It is to identify concentrations and feedback loops that may make some claims sociologically difficult to falsify or some alternatives unable to receive a serious test.

Counterfactual analysis can estimate how decisions change when status signals are altered, while qualitative research examines why participants rely on those signals. The audit should preserve legitimate explanations such as rare expertise or facility access and distinguish them from inherited visibility. It should also expose the pedigree of AI systems: their training corpora, platform ownership, benchmark communities, and model lineages. An automated evaluator can reproduce hierarchy even when names are hidden because prestige remains encoded in citation structure and textual style.

These projects require mixed methods. Large-scale bibliometric and network analysis can identify concentration, but it cannot determine fairness or scientific significance by itself. Controlled review experiments can test blinding, structured criteria, and alternative funding mechanisms. Ethnographic and interview work can reveal how scientists actually use AI systems, where authority shifts, and which forms of oversight become ceremonial. Institutional prototypes can test appeal, minority reports, negative-result credit, and benefit-sharing in real collaborations.

Institutional simulation can examine how small changes in incentives alter long-term scientific diversity. Models can compare publication rewards, replication budgets, threshold lotteries, portfolio diversity constraints, open failure archives, and different intellectual-property regimes. Such simulations do not predict institutions mechanically. They generate hypotheses and reveal hidden assumptions for field experiments. The relevant outcomes include concentration, correction time, survival of minority programmes, duplicated effort, reproducibility, and the distribution of risk and benefit.

An anti-monoculture monitor should analyze common dependencies across a portfolio. A hundred projects may use different titles while relying on the same foundation model, benchmark, ontology, data provider, and evaluation rule. Conversely, two superficially similar projects may explore genuinely different mechanisms. The monitor should represent this difference and help allocate resources to independent evaluators, alternative datasets, underexplored populations, and competing representations. It should not become a novelty score that researchers learn to game.

The human-command constitution should be expressed as operational rights. People must know which decisions are theirs, receive evidence in a form suitable to those decisions, possess adequate time and competence, be able to stop or revise the process, and have access to an appeal path. A click-to-approve interface does not meet this condition. Nor does a committee that is formally responsible but lacks access to the relevant provenance or the power to change the system. The research question is whether authority can be made both effective and compatible with substantial local machine autonomy.

Appeal must be designed as part of the architecture rather than added after a controversial decision. Affected researchers and communities need access to the relevant evidence, dependency graph, policy basis, and decision history. The appeal body must possess authority to change the result and protection from the same conflicts that shaped the original decision. Research should measure correction, delay, accessibility, strategic abuse, and whether weaker actors can use the process in practice rather than only in principle.

Benefit attribution can be prototyped alongside contribution tracking. A project can record public funding, data contributions, community agreements, software and model ownership, laboratory labor, environmental cost, intellectual property, and downstream licensing. The infrastructure does not choose a distributive theory, but it makes the consequences of alternative rules visible. A human-governed automated science that accelerates discovery while concentrating all benefits in the owners of orchestration infrastructure would fail the programme's political objective even if its technical components worked.

This project family should be rejected or substantially revised if its audits become new centralized reputation scores, if blinding reduces necessary accountability, if portfolio diversity protects indefensible work indefinitely, or if human command remains ceremonial. The success criterion is not social equality detached from scientific performance. It is a more contestable system in which expertise remains usable, evidence can overcome pedigree more often, independent alternatives survive long enough to be tested, and consequential automation remains subject to legitimate control.

The final project family concerns the constitution of the system. Institutional experiments must test whether evidence-first interfaces, portfolio diversity, appeal, decision rights, credit, and benefit can counteract pedigree and concentration without pretending that social power can be reduced to one neutral score.

The first programme objective is not to build every component simultaneously. It is to create a thin, end-to-end demonstrator in which a research question becomes a living specification, expands into several bounded branches, executes through heterogeneous tools, returns evidence into a claim graph, receives independent criticism, and produces a signed view with a validity dossier. The demonstrator should be small enough to understand completely and rich enough to expose the interfaces that matter.

A practical initial demonstrator can reuse available workbench, provenance, agent, sandbox, and evaluation components without treating any one stack as canonical. The first domain should favour digital reproducibility while still requiring nontrivial judgment. Candidate use cases include novelty analysis, specification-to-experiment traceability, automated validity dossiers, controlled evidence sharing, and independent replication of a bounded result.

The book-to-prototype use case is especially appropriate for ScriptaHub. A research-programme chapter is decomposed into DS0XX specifications. Coding agents propose implementations and tests inside sandboxes. A critic checks alignment between prose commitments, design documents, and code. The workbench records divergences and updates the high-level research object. Success would not be the automatic production of software from prose. It would be the ability to detect semantic drift and make revision cheaper than silent divergence.

A novelty demonstrator should compare several grounding paths while preserving the same task definition, corpus boundary, and auditable comparison logic: A peer-review demonstrator should decompose review into citation, method, code, statistics, novelty, ethical scope, and domain relevance. Agents and tools return typed reports before seeing one another's conclusions. The system displays dependency fingerprints and routes unresolved questions to humans. A compliance demonstrator can attach privacy, copyright, and organizational policies to the same object, showing that scientific validity and permission are related but distinct dimensions.

Later demonstrators can connect to autonomous laboratory platforms, formal proof environments, or distributed privacy-preserving computation. Each integration should occur through a narrow evidence contract. The programme should resist building a large interface catalogue before a few contracts have survived real correction. Interoperability must grow from demonstrated exchanges, not from speculative completeness.

Every demonstrator should include a control condition that omits the proposed architecture. The book-to-prototype experiment can compare a specification-driven repository with a direct coding-agent workflow. The novelty experiment can compare structured representations with strong semantic-search baselines. The review experiment can compare decomposed critics with a single expert model and with human review. The privacy experiment can compare traceable protected execution with conventional data export. Without such controls, a sophisticated stack can attribute to itself benefits produced by the underlying models or by extra human attention.

The demonstrations should share a small common data model: project identity, specification clause, artefact identity, claim, evidence packet, critic verdict, decision, and provenance event. This common nucleus is more important than a large universal ontology. Domain extensions can add estimands, assays, proof objects, consent conditions, or interpretive codes. If the common nucleus proves too weak, extensions will reveal the missing relation. If it is too heavy, user behaviour will reveal which fields are ceremonial and should be removed.

User research is part of the technical programme. Non-IT researchers should be able to understand the current state of an inquiry, identify unresolved obligations, and approve consequential transformations without reading orchestration code. Software engineers should be able to reproduce executions and locate semantic requirements. Reviewers should be able to navigate from a claim to the smallest relevant evidence slice. Partners should be able to contribute a bounded component without receiving unrestricted access to the whole project. These interaction requirements are falsifiable and should shape the prototype from the beginning.

The first vertical slice should also expose costs. The workbench must report model calls, compute, human review time, failed branches, storage, and correction latency. Automation that reduces coding time while multiplying review and integration effort may still be worthwhile, but the trade-off must be visible. This is particularly important for coding agents: their apparent implementation speed can hide preparation, test construction, security review, dependency repair, and long-term maintenance. A complete demonstrator measures the entire research trajectory, not only the fastest local operation.

Finally, the demonstrator should produce communication artefacts for different audiences from the same research object. Researchers need the detailed specification and evidence graph. Managers and partners need scope, dependencies, maturity, and unresolved risks. Funders need objectives, work packages, hypotheses, and measurable outcomes. Public or regulatory audiences need consequence, uncertainty, authority, and rights. Generating these views from one maintained object is a practical test of whether the programme can reduce internal and external semantic drift.

Figure 35. The book-to-specification-to-evidence cycle. Faster implementation increases the need for preparation, evaluator design, and independent validation.

Forecasts about AI are unreliable, especially when they assume smooth scaling. The following scenarios are not predictions of model capability alone. They are conditional projections based on current technical trajectories, the economics of research, and the slow adaptation of institutions. Their purpose is to clarify what infrastructure choices matter. By 2030, persistent scientific copilots are likely to be ordinary in computationally intensive fields. They will be connected to institutional repositories, literature services, code environments, and data platforms. A project will have a living specification and a machine-maintained map of claims, evidence, and tasks. Agents will propose and implement analyses, rerun affected branches after changes, and assemble reproducibility packages. Human researchers will review diffs and claim transitions rather than reading every generated token. The most visible change will be that the manuscript is generated late from a maintained research state rather than used as the place where the project state is assembled. Results, methods, and citations will be synchronized with artefacts. Journals will increasingly accept or require machine-readable research packages. Automated preflight will become similar to continuous integration: a submission that lacks environment capture, claim-evidence links, or baseline accounting will fail before human review in fields where these requirements are feasible. Coding-agent techniques will transfer directly. Laboratories will maintain project instructions, specialized skills, hooks, and eval suites.

A change to a dataset or analysis function will trigger relevant tests and identify affected claims. The scientific analogue of a pull request will present not only file diffs but epistemic diffs: assumptions changed, evidence added, claim narrowed, critic disagreement unresolved. Reviewers will operate on this change set. By 2030, the strongest systems will still be heterogeneous and supervised. Formal and computational branches will have high local autonomy. Literature and information workflows will be largely automated but audited. Laboratory planning will be common, while physical execution autonomy will remain concentrated in facilities with standardized instruments. Clinical and social research will use copilots extensively for analysis and protocol support but maintain strong human and regulatory gates. By 2035, research workbenches are likely to coordinate networks rather than single projects. Machine-readable capability descriptions will allow systems to allocate simulations, analyses, and experiments across laboratories and cloud services. Inter-laboratory replication can be triggered automatically for claims that reach a specified stage or show high common-mode risk. Evidence objects will accumulate across institutions while preserving local access control. Portfolio science will become more explicit. A major research programme may maintain hundreds of branches, but only a small number will receive expensive evidence. Agents will estimate expected information gain, cost, risk, and diversity. Negative results will update shared models and prevent redundant work.

Funding agencies may support portfolios as versioned programmes rather than evaluate only fixed proposals and final papers. Neuro-symbolic and domain-specific interpreters will become more important than ever-larger monolithic agents. The easiest gains from general language capability will have been captured. Reliability will depend on tool-specific validators, typed representations, causal models, proof systems, and instrument models. Scientific runtimes will route tasks according to evidence requirements. The term “agent” may become less central as adaptive components are embedded inside ordinary research infrastructure. Peer review will be continuous for evidence objects. A paper can remain the citable public argument, but claims will receive updates from replication, reanalysis, or new evidence. Journals and repositories may display evidence maturity and unresolved dissent rather than a binary published status. Machine assistance will reduce routine checks, but specialist attention will remain scarce and may become a separately funded activity. By 2040, limited autonomous research programmes are plausible in domains with strong evaluators, digital execution, and manageable risk. A system may maintain a long-lived objective, generate and prune branches, allocate compute, produce proofs or algorithms, and release low-risk results under a standing policy. Some autonomous laboratories may operate continuously within tightly defined chemical, materials, or biological spaces. The important qualifier is limited. The objective, risk envelope, evidence profile, and release authority will be externally governed. A universal autonomous scientist is less probable.

Science contains too many heterogeneous regimes and contested objectives. Even very capable models will operate through institutions, instruments, data rights, and public consequences. The more plausible endpoint is institutional autonomy: a human-machine organization capable of maintaining inquiry over long periods, revising its representations, and producing evidence-bearing outputs. Intelligence resides in the architecture and governance as much as in any model. Several developments could slow or redirect these scenarios. Model progress may plateau on long-horizon reliability. Compute and energy may constrain broad search. Data access and copyright disputes may limit literature integration. Laboratories may resist standardization. Research fraud may exploit automated infrastructure faster than governance adapts. Public backlash may restrict autonomous experimentation. Conversely, breakthroughs in theorem proving, causal modelling, robotics, or persistent memory could accelerate specific domains. The key uncertainty is not whether AI can produce impressive scientific episodes. It is whether institutions can absorb them. Universities and journals change more slowly than software platforms. Incentives may continue to reward papers rather than evidence objects. Proprietary systems may fragment standards. Researchers may reject heavy workflow structure. The transition will likely be uneven, with leading computational and industrial laboratories adopting workbenches long before many disciplines. The most important forecast is therefore architectural: scientific results will migrate from documents into versioned systems. This migration is already beginning through repositories, notebooks, data packages, preregistrations, and automated workflows.

AI increases the pressure because the

volume and speed of transformations make informal memory inadequate. Whether the systems are called

scientific workbenches, research operating systems, evidence graphs, or laboratory copilots, their function will be to preserve the state of inquiry outside the model’s conversation.

Future projects should be organized around falsifiable slices of the architecture rather than around the vague objective of building an artificial scientist. One consortium may study executable research specifications and scientific workbenches. Another may focus on novelty, idea lineage, and cross-domain transfer. Others may address automated peer review, compliance, privacy-preserving research, autonomous laboratories, formal verification, or institutional incentives. The common research object and evidence model allow these projects to contribute to one programme without requiring one monolithic grant or organization.

ScriptaHub's role can vary. In some projects it may lead the workbench and orchestration architecture. In others it may contribute a work package on specifications, agent governance, novelty, privacy, or evaluation. The programme is designed to make such contributions legible to external partners and to prevent local deliverables from drifting away from the larger vision. Design specifications, demonstrators, benchmark datasets, and validity dossiers should become portable collaboration objects.

Several issues remain deliberately open. The programme does not assume one final controlled language, one universal ontology, one model provider, one vector representation, one novelty metric, or one autonomy level. It does not assume that all scientific disciplines should converge on the same workbench interface. It does not know whether a generalized a governed interpretation runtime will outperform simpler orchestration, whether operational ideas can be represented with sufficient intersubjective stability, or how far automated agents can participate in normative and interpretive inquiry. These are research questions, not omissions to be hidden.

The human future is open as well. People may remain principal investigators, become governors of agent communities, specialize as critics and institutional designers, or collaborate with machine-generated concepts that are only partially interpretable. The programme insists only on a constitutional minimum: consequential goals and releases must remain contestable; evidence and dependency must remain inspectable; affected people must retain meaningful standing; and the benefits of accelerated science should not be captured solely by the owners of the infrastructure.

this revision should therefore be read as an invitation to correction. Its best possible outcome is not that every component is built as described. It is that the programme allows ScriptaHub and its partners to discover, early and explicitly, which components are necessary, which are redundant, which claims are wrong, and which unexplored combinations deserve sustained research. The frontier remains correction because a programme capable of revising itself is more valuable than a roadmap that merely predicts its own success.

An integrated first programme should remain deliberately narrow. One demonstrator can use a digitally native research task: a computational study with literature search, code generation, execution, claim extraction, independent rerun, novelty analysis, and peer review. A second can connect to a bounded laboratory or instrument simulator. A third can examine a socially consequential domain in which the main output is not autonomous action but a validity dossier and decision-rights workflow. Together these cases test different forms of resistance without requiring a universal scientific platform.

The programme should be revised when its own concepts fail. If claim-evidence graphs do not improve inspection, the representation must change. If semantic diffs are too unstable for experts to trust, they should not become release gates. If novelty residuals collapse under corpus expansion, the method should be abandoned or restricted. If dependency fingerprints fail to predict correlated error, independence must be represented differently. If human review becomes ceremonial, autonomy must be reduced or the interface and institution redesigned. The architecture earns credibility only by exposing its own assumptions to the same corrective principles it proposes for science.

The long-term objective is not the maximum automation of every scientific act. It is the maximum responsible delegation compatible with plural inquiry, independent resistance, human welfare, and legitimate control of consequence. Machines should search more broadly, execute more reliably, preserve more memory, and expose more error. Humans should not be reduced to ceremonial approval. They should steer purposes, challenge representations, decide what consequences are acceptable, protect those who bear risk, and share in the benefits generated by the scientific system.

Epilogue. The Frontier Remains Correction

A research programme is useful only while it remains easier to correct than the institutions and infrastructures it may eventually create. The final reflection therefore returns to the relation

between authorship, automation, responsibility, and the public record.

Epilogue. Science After the Author

Artificial intelligence radicalizes this ideal and reveals its limits. A claim can emerge without a single human author in the traditional sense. It may be produced by a foundation model, a retrieval system, a planning agent, a code generator, a robotic instrument, a laboratory operator, several datasets, and a set of validators. Who had the idea? The person who chose the question, the model that connected two literatures, the agent that framed the hypothesis, the engineers who built the system, the authors of the

sources, or the community that supplied decisive validation? Romantic authorship dissolves into

genealogy.

Responsibility must not dissolve with it. The more distributed the production of knowledge becomes, the more precisely attribution should be reconstructed. We can abandon the fiction of one sovereign mind without abandoning the trail. Credit for generation can be separated from credit for validation, from ownership of infrastructure, and from responsibility for use. Artificial systems can receive explicit attribution as contributors without being treated as moral authorities or convenient containers for blame.

The history told in this book supports a simple thesis: science is more than a method and less than an oracle. It is an institutional culture of corrigible knowledge. Philosophy supplied questions about justification and the limits of certainty. Alchemy supplied techniques, material discipline, and a warning about secrecy. Learned societies turned testimony into public practice. Instruments and standards made observations comparable. Statistics disciplined the appetite for patterns. Peer review created an imperfect filter. The reproducibility crisis showed that incentives, transparency, and organizational design belong inside methodology. AI does not erase this history. It compresses and accelerates it.

The first generations of artificial research systems already occupy almost every stage of the scientific cycle. They retrieve and screen literature, build evidence-linked syntheses, generate hypotheses, write and test code, design experiments, operate laboratories, interpret data, and draft papers. None is a universal autonomous scientist. Their competence is jagged: striking within a structured environment, fragile under distribution shift, poor at recognizing when the task itself has been misconceived, and vulnerable to evaluators that reward the appearance of success. The correct conclusion is neither dismissal nor surrender. It is that capability and legitimacy must be engineered separately.

In the coming decades, agents will become genuine partners. Some will propose hypotheses no human team would have found. Some will operate laboratories over timescales and design spaces inaccessible to ordinary practice. Some will produce mathematical objects, causal structures, or machine-native concepts that resist immediate translation. They will sometimes fail in banal ways. At other times their failure will be so distributed and internally coherent that it will escape detection for years. Novelty will become cheap. The rare achievement will be a result accompanied by sufficient reasons to believe it.

For that reason, the central scientific infrastructure of the future may not be the largest model. It may be the validity dossier: the live relation among claim, evidence, process, independence, intended use, and contestation. Storing more logs is not enough. Independence must be organized. A debate among copies of one model is not replication. A digital signature is not empirical truth. A benchmark score is not a safety case. A fluent uncertainty statement is not calibrated uncertainty. Each technical mechanism contributes only when embedded in an ecology of criticism.

Science may reach a point at which no human understands every internal transformation, yet people understand the conditions under which the result remains robust. We already accept weaker forms of this compromise in particle physics, climate modelling, genomics, and large software systems. It can be legitimate when interfaces expose assumptions, interventions test predictions, independent groups reproduce results, and failures remain traceable. It becomes dangerous when complexity is used as a reason to demand obedience.

Predictive validity does not choose an end. A system can forecast disease while reproducing an unjust category. It can optimize crop yield while concentrating ownership. It can discover an efficient synthesis while increasing ecological risk. It can rank promising questions while narrowing collective curiosity. A civilization can delegate calculation without delegating meaning. The question what works cannot absorb the questions for whom, at what cost, under whose authority, and toward which form of life.

The artificial partner will therefore force science to say what it values in itself. If we value only prediction and control, we will build optimization engines and call them scientists. If we also value public reasons, freedom of criticism, plural inquiry, calibrated abstention, and the obligation to correct, we will build something different: a science wider than any human mind and still constrained by a human ethics of doubt.

This ethics is not a claim that human beings must occupy every step. It is a claim that knowledge with public consequences must remain answerable to beings who live with those consequences. Artificial agents can extend perception, memory, search, and invention. They can also help expose human complacency, institutional ritual, and prestige disguised as evidence. Their greatest contribution may not be to replace the scientist but to make visible how much science has always depended on distributed cognition, tacit infrastructure, and organized trust.

In the first room, a person watched the crucible and hoped that matter would disclose its secret. In the second, an agent searches a space of possibilities too large for us to survey. Between those rooms does not stand the triumph of intelligence alone. It stands the invention of responsibility: the long, unfinished effort to make power answer to evidence and evidence answer to criticism.

Perhaps the deepest transformation will be science after the author. The modern article taught us to attach a claim to a name, an institution, and a coherent narrative. In research distributed among people, agents, instruments, and databases, the single author becomes an increasingly strained fiction. Yet accountability can be rebuilt around decisions: who chose the question, who authorized the risk, who preserved the evidence, who tested the result, who benefited, and who can stop its use.

A dignified relationship with artificial research partners requires neither worship nor denial. We need not attribute genius to benefit from their power, and we need not erase their contribution to protect human pride. We can accept that some discoveries will be found in spaces we cannot explore manually, that some theories will first appear foreign, and that some campaigns will exceed the capacity of every individual. At the same time, we can refuse to turn performance into sovereignty.

In the old workshop, the fire illuminated only the face of the practitioner. In the laboratory of the future, sensors and records can illuminate every consequential step, but only if we choose to preserve the trail and open it to challenge. Between secrecy and verification, speed and understanding, the optimal and the good, the next form of science will be decided.

Technical Synthesis: Correction as the Frontier

The technical survey reaches the same institutional conclusion from another direction.

The history of machine learning is often narrated as an expansion of what can be generated or predicted. The next phase may be better understood as an expansion of what can be corrected. A system becomes scientifically useful when its errors are not merely punished by a benchmark but converted into evidence about representations, assumptions, instruments and questions. The decisive capability is not permanent confidence. It is organized revisability.

Novelty enters this process as a provisional mismatch. A candidate differs from a record, distribution, class or theory. The system then asks which interpretation is warranted. Is the mismatch noise, drift, an unknown class, a new mechanism or a duplicate under another description? Each answer implies a different test. The novelty detector is therefore only the first sensor in a longer epistemic loop.

Structural limits remain. No model can create information that has no trace, choose uniquely among observationally identical worlds or certify global priority from an incomplete archive. These limits are useful because they force better questions. They motivate interventions, new sensors, scoped claims and explicit assumptions. Intelligence is partly the ability to identify when the problem must be changed.

Movable boundaries remain equally important. Models can become better calibrated under shift. Representations can become more causal and modular. Continual learning can preserve provenance. World models can expose uncertainty. Search can become more diverse. Scientific agents can learn to seek refutation and revise beliefs. Laboratories can automate controls, replication and semantic provenance. These advances do not abolish epistemology; they implement it.

The most reliable discoveries described in this survey share an architecture. A generator proposes more than one possibility. A search process explores. An evaluator provides independent resistance. An archive preserves alternatives and lineage. Experiments connect the system to the world. Institutions decide which results enter the record. Remove any one component and apparent discovery can become fluent speculation, benchmark gaming or untraceable automation.

This architecture also explains why humans are unlikely to disappear from science in one clean step. Human roles move as tools strengthen. Formal checking delegates proof verification. Autonomous laboratories delegate execution and some experiment selection. Literature systems delegate retrieval and synthesis. Humans continue to reframe questions, negotiate significance, inspect anomalies and govern consequences. Future systems may automate more of these roles, but the need for independent perspectives will remain even if their implementation changes.

The deepest novelty may not be a molecule, theorem or algorithm. It may be a new scientific institution in which machine-readable claims, executable evidence, autonomous experiments, formal verifiers and human judgment form one revisable network. Such an institution could make replication routine, negative results reusable and disagreement computationally productive. It could also centralize attention and reproduce shared blind spots. Its design is therefore a scientific and political question.

A good discovery machine should be difficult to impress and easy to correct. It should distinguish unfamiliarity from importance, confidence from evidence and execution from understanding. It should report the boundary of its claim. It should know which external test has authority and preserve the failures that led to revision. It should expand the search space without expanding the space of untraceable assertions at the same rate.

The frontier of novelty is not reached when generation becomes limitless. It is reached when criticism, verification and revision become equally scalable.

That frontier is attainable in pieces. The work now is to connect those pieces while keeping their epistemic roles distinct. Machine learning can help science discover more, but its greatest contribution may be to make the path from surprise to knowledge more explicit than it has ever been.

The architecture of executable science adds one final implication: the manuscript remains necessary, but it no longer stands alone.

The scientific paper will survive the arrival of research agents for the same reason that source code did not eliminate design documents and legal records did not eliminate public argument. Human communities need narratives that explain what matters. A graph of claims and evidence can preserve structure, but it does not select significance. A reproducible workflow can show how an output was produced, but it cannot decide why the result deserves attention. A theorem prover can certify a statement, but it cannot determine whether the statement changes a field. The paper remains the place where researchers accept responsibility for an intelligible interpretation.

What changes is its monopoly. The manuscript can no longer carry the whole burden of scientific memory when machines generate and transform research artefacts at a speed that exceeds human reconstruction. The result must live in a larger object: versioned, evidence-bearing, and partially executable. The paper becomes a signed view over that object. A reviewer can inspect the route from claim to evidence. A replicator can rerun the relevant branch. A future agent can learn from a negative result. An institution can see who authorized release. A community can preserve disagreement without rewriting history.

This infrastructure makes science more software-like, but the analogy stops at the point where the world, interpretation, and authority resist formal closure. Software is judged against purposes that can often be stated before implementation. Research frequently changes the language of its purpose. The specification is living. A successful experiment can revise the hypothesis, the evaluator, or the question. Executable science must therefore preserve the ability to change frames rather than merely optimize within them.

That is why the central risk is not an intelligent machine but a mechanical loop. Any system can become mechanical when it continues to optimize a proxy after the proxy has lost contact with the purpose of inquiry. A model can optimize plausible prose. A benchmark community can optimize scores. A journal can optimize citation and throughput. A researcher can optimize publication count. The appropriate defence is meta-rational: representations, evaluators, and decision rights must remain revisable under evidence.

Specification-driven inquiry provides one architecture for this defence. It separates persistent intent from transient prompts. It creates a ladder from mission to claim, protocol, artefact, and release. It explodes one specification into a portfolio of constructive and adversarial branches. It places deterministic pipelines around adaptive local agents. It treats skills as interpreters that declare assumptions and evidence. It promotes claims through new kinds of support rather than through repeated self-confidence. It makes stopping, disagreement, and negative results first-class outcomes.

No single project can implement this entire vision. Existing research and engineering already provide structured generation, workflow systems, reusable agent capabilities, tool interfaces, sandboxes, provenance standards, research-object packaging, preregistration, reproducible notebooks, proof assistants, causal models, and autonomous laboratories. The programme proposed here concerns their missing epistemic integration: how intent, evidence, criticism, decision rights, and revision can remain connected while implementations vary. The future should be built by composing, testing, and simplifying these mechanisms rather than by declaring a universal technical stack in advance.

The most valuable scientific copilot will not be the one that sounds most like a scientist. It will be the one that helps a research group preserve intent, design stronger tests, expose semantic drift, reproduce results, allocate attention, and correct itself. It will know when to invoke a language model and when to avoid one. It will not confuse an executable result with a justified claim. It will make authority visible and leave room for contest.

The human role becomes more demanding, not ceremonial. Researchers will formulate purposes, choose representations, build or select evaluators, interpret resistance from the world, and take responsibility for release. They will need to understand less of every implementation detail and more about the boundaries of each delegated regime. Institutions will need to reward maintenance, replication, negative results, and decisive criticism. Education will need to cultivate diagnostic judgment rather than routine production.

The old record is already strained by repositories, notebooks, data stores, instruments, and conversations; generative systems multiply the transformations. Science therefore needs a versioned operational substrate or it will accept consequential results produced through processes no one can reconstruct.

The desirable future is accountable acceleration: local agents explore, external evaluators resist, specialists judge bounded questions, institutions authorize consequence, and the research object remembers why claims changed. Publication becomes a release, not an ending. Evidence continues to arrive; claims can be narrowed, strengthened, reproduced, contested, or superseded.

Science becomes executable when it can show not only what it concluded, but what would make it conclude otherwise.

Additional Selected References for the Research Programme

The references below combine foundations in philosophy and sociology of science with technical work relevant to research objects, provenance, neuro-symbolic systems, agentic science, formal verification, autonomous laboratories, privacy, reproducibility, and the political economy of scientific institutions. They are routes into the claims of the programme rather than a claim of exhaustive coverage.
